## `#325` `#326` `#327` — THE ABSENCE CONTRACT NEVER REACHED THE PROTOTYPE, AND `#322` FIXED ONE HOME OF A TWO-HOME SENTENCE

Found by looking at a render and by an adversarial pass, not by re-reading. Both of the things
that found these were instruments I had not yet pointed at the question.

### `#325` — `pc()` had TWO holes, and `#320` claimed to have closed one of them

`shared.js:41` read `const pc = p => \`var(--${(p || "k").toLowerCase()})\`;`. Measured by
calling the page's OWN `pc()` in Chromium against the shipped build:

| call | returned | resolved to | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pc('RB')` | `var(--rb)` | `#0ca89c` | correct |
| `pc('')` / `pc(null)` | `var(--k)` | `#fab87e` | **the KICKER's real colour** |
| `pc('XYZ')` | `var(--xyz)` | `#f2ead9` | **`--ink` — the colour of the text** |

The first hole is the pre-`#311` fallback that `POSITION_PILL_ABSENT` was created to end. **The
second was not in the original diagnosis and is worse**: an unknown position is not falsy, so it
never reaches the `|| "k"` branch and asks for a variable that does not exist. That is invalid at
computed-value time, so the element INHERITS — a pill wearing the colour of the prose around it,
which is exactly the condition `#311`'s quiet-text rule exists to forbid.

**`#320` emitted `--absent` and nothing read it.** A grep for any consumer returns empty. So this
claim in `#320`'s own docstring was false as shipped, and is corrected rather than dropped:

> "`--absent` is emitted too, because `#311` gave the absence marker its own token and the
> prototype has no word for it: an unmapped position there still falls back to a POSITION's
> colour, **which is the defect `POSITION_PILL_ABSENT` exists to end.**"

Emitting a variable nothing reads ends nothing. The repair uses CSS's own `var()` fallback, so no
list of known positions is duplicated into JS (`#126`):

```js
const pc = p => `var(--${(p || "absent").toLowerCase()}, var(--absent))`;
```

After: `pc(null)` → `#a79a83`, `pc('XYZ')` → `#a79a83`, `pc('RB')` → the RB pill. Mutation arms,
run against scratch copies of all 8 built pages so the repo tree stayed clean:

| arm | failures |
|---|---|
| unmutated | 0 |
| revert to `(p \|\| "k")` | **3** |
| keep `"absent"` but drop the `var(…, var(--absent))` tail | **1** — only the unknown-position arm |

The test calls `pc()` itself rather than re-deriving what it should return (`#222`).

### `#326` — a false assertion in the palette's one home, recorded at `#311` and never repaired

`design_system.py:97` stated: *"amber-b sits >= 39.8 from every position pill it shares a roster
row with (TE is the nearest; it was 57.2 from gold-b)."* Measured today:

```
  K   33.17   <-- NEAREST, and BELOW the asserted 39.8
  TE  46.78     IDP 49.15     DEF 91.48 ... rest 91.5-141.1
  amber-b vs crimson-b = 68.97  ("69.0" still holds)
```

Both halves false. **The rule never broke** — `test_design_system.py:269` enforces **25.0**, and
33.17 clears it comfortably. What broke is the SHAPE of the prose: it wrote an OBSERVED MARGIN in
the grammar of a GUARANTEE, so it read as a contract and rotted the moment a pill moved. That is
`#56` ("a bound is not a threshold") applied to a sentence.

`#311` moved K, **recorded this exact breakage at `POST_AUDIT_PLAN.md:16948`, and never changed
the file.** `#318` then moved TE, so both surviving figures described a hex that exists nowhere in
the repo. The margins are therefore REMOVED rather than updated — updating them only schedules
the next rot. The floor is a constant and stays in the comment; the margins are measured by the
test that enforces them. `test_design_system.py:265` carried the same defect in milder form: its
hedge ("measured when the move was made") scoped the NUMBER to history but left the IDENTITY
("TE is the nearest") in the present tense, and the identity rotted too.

### `#327` — `MAIN_PAGE.md` is the second home of the sentence `#322` repaired

`MAIN_PAGE.md:157-160` carries, in the present tense, the identical claim `#322` fixed in
`_palette.py`: six entries, a fallback to K's neutral, "a capability the prototype has and the app
does not". `#322` repaired one home and nobody grepped for the other — **`#126` sitting underneath
the stale-prose defect**. Struck in place with its evidence, per house style, not rewritten.

Two more in the same document:

- the pill divergence table (`#8f86f0` as "app QB"; "app NO ENTRY" for DL/LB/DB, which have had
  entries since `#311`) — after `#320` all ten measure **dE 0.00** prototype-vs-app.
- **"37 prototype tokens"** → now **27**. `#320` moved the ten pills out of the prototype's
  `:root`; 37 − 10 = 27 exactly.

### A CORRECTION I OWE THE ADVERSARIAL PASS

The agent reported the token count as 27. I ran a regex of my own over the same file, got **32**,
and published that its figure was wrong. **Mine was wrong.** My regex counted `--f-d`, `--f-m`,
`--f-s`, `--r` and `--hatch` — fonts, a radius and an rgba — as colour tokens. `_palette.py`
already computes this number and reports 27.

I reconstructed a quantity the instrument computes, got a different answer, and used the
reconstruction to overrule the instrument — the precise error `#222` cost two withdrawn findings
to learn, committed while writing up a batch about that error. The figure published above is read
from `_palette.py`'s output.

### Verified

```
pc(null) #a79a83   pc('XYZ') #a79a83   pc('RB') the RB pill  (measured in Chromium)
135 targeted tests across 6 modules: OK
mutation arms: 0 / 3 / 1 as tabled above
all seven ratchets PASS; floors 242 modules / 7605 assertions
```

- **`#328` — `mockups/`**, verified and deliberately NOT taken in this batch. `c_variants.py:394`

  DL/LB/DB: "#a09480" }` in SOURCE, so no rebuild repairs it — four superseded hexes, no IDP, and

## `#314` `#319` `#319b` — A SUM UNDER A PER-CALL FIELD'S NAME, AND A STRUCK SPEC WITH THREE MORE HOMES

### `#314` — `totals()` published a number no call took

`provider_meter.totals()` returned `latency_ms` as `round(sum(...))` guarded by `any()`, sitting
three lines below two token fields guarded by `all()`, and spelled **exactly like
`CallRecord.latency_ms`, the PER-CALL field**. Three calls at 100ms, 300ms and one unmeasured
returned **400.0**, and no call took 400ms. The function's own docstring forbids this eleven lines
above: *"a number that reads as authoritative and is not, which is the failure mode a cost display
cannot afford."*

**Deleted, not redefined.** A consumer written against the old key would have changed meaning
without changing shape — the most expensive kind of silent break. Nothing outside tests read it
(verified by grep), so the key is gone and a stale consumer gets a `KeyError`. Replaced by:

- `latency_ms_slowest` — ONE REAL CALL's measurement, so partial data makes it less
  representative but never fictional
- `latency_reported` — how partial it was

**An end-to-end SPAN is deliberately not offered.** The user waits on a whole debate, not one
chair's call (`DRAFT_ROOM_UI.md:176`), but `CallRecord` stores no start timestamp, so a span
cannot be derived from what exists. Naming the gap is honest; summing overlapping calls to invent
one would be this same defect wearing a new key.

Mutation arms, run against in-memory recompiles of the module so the tree stayed clean:

| arm | result |
|---|---|
| unmutated | silent |
| restore the original `round(sum(...))` | **FIRES** (1 failure + 1 error) |
| `max(...)` → `sum(...)` | **FIRES** |
| `any(...)` → `all(...)` on the slowest | **FIRES** |

### `#319` — §14's band specification struck, and `#319b` — it had three more homes

Owner ruled the phrase *"without the meh grouping"* banned the BAND, not a variant. §14's band
section is struck in place, kept unedited because its measurement work is real.

**Then the same mechanism as everything else today.** Ten `.md` files cite §14. Rather than
assume all ten were stale — §14 is a large section and only its band subsection was struck — the
population was narrowed to citations that actually make a BAND claim. Five, and they needed four
different treatments:

| site | verdict |
|---|---|
| `fableA/RATIONALE.md:146` | **already correct** — it says "no bands" |
| `POST_AUDIT_PLAN.md:10882` | register history, correct as history |
| `DRAFT_ROOM_UI.md:423` (U22) | a RULED answer to a question that no longer arises → marked MOOT |
| `DRAFT_ROOM_UI.md:1024` | **the conclusion survives, the reason does not** |
| `fableB/RATIONALE.md:325` | a different variant's lineage — recorded, not unilaterally rewritten |

**`:1024` is the one worth stating.** It read *"THE FORMAT IS ON SCREEN AT ALL TIMES... §14's
bands are derived from the league's own scoring."* The bands were the stated REASON for a rule the
built surface still obeys. Striking them would have left a live rule justified by a refused
mechanism — but deleting the rule would have been worse. The tank is league-derived whether or not
it is banded, because what it spans is the position's PRICED POOL. So the reason is restated and
the conclusion kept.

**A claim whose stated reason is withdrawn is not automatically false.** Treating it as false
would have removed a rule the built surface obeys. That is the inverse of the error this register
usually records, and it is worth naming because the reflex built up over today's items —
"the sentence is stale, strike it" — would have produced exactly it.

After `#319b`, the only `§14`+band matches left in `DRAFT_ROOM_UI.md` are the two markers
themselves.

## `#315` — THE HULL EXTRACTION THAT FOUND AN UNTESTED FUNCTION, AND THE RATCHET THAT REFUSED IT

`build_pick_ledger` lifted out of `app.py:1712-1726` into `pick_ledger.py`, by AST span rather
than by retyping, the way `#300` lifted `build_freshness_manifest`. Function body verified
**byte-identical** against `git show HEAD:app.py`.

The hull imports the NAME, not the module, and that form is load-bearing:
`test_league_view_wiring` asserts the literal call site `pick_ledger = build_pick_ledger(snapshot)`
appears exactly once in each of two blocks, so `import pick_ledger` would have rewritten those
call sites to `pick_ledger.build_pick_ledger(...)` and failed both. There is also a latent
collision the name-import avoids: the new module is `pick_ledger.py` and the local variable at
every call site is `pick_ledger`.

### `api_surface` refused the extraction, which is the whole reason it exists

```
UNASSIGNED MODULE: pick_ledger -- the hull reaches it and no layer claims it.
Decide whose job it is (ENGINE / ORCHESTRATION / PRODUCT_STORE / ADMIN / RENDER)
and record the evidence, or route the reach away.
```

`#310` built this ratchet on the principle that the ASSIGNMENT is the thing that must not go
stale. A new module entering the hull is a new ownership decision, and it would not let one
through unmade. **Assigned ENGINE, on four pieces of evidence rather than by feel:**

1. Its nearest sibling is already there — `player_universe` owns *"the pool and league
   OWNERSHIP"*, and this answers the same kind of question about a future pick.
2. It prices nothing. Its own docstring refuses to, and `estimate_future_pick_value` is a
   separate ruling — so it does not reach into valuation.
3. No credentials, no I/O, no writes. That rules out `ORCHESTRATION` (which holds provider
   credentials) and `PRODUCT_STORE` (per-league state a person reads AND WRITES).
4. The structural precedent is exact: `freshness` was lifted from the same hull by `#300` and
   assigned ENGINE on the reasoning that a hull-liftable derivation over league facts IS engine
   work. `#85`'s future-pick valuation waits on this one as an INPUT.

The draft room's slice is unchanged at 15 engine functions in 7 modules — correctly, since this
feeds the league view, not the draft room.

### THE FINDING: THE FUNCTION HAD NO BEHAVIOUR TEST

The only test naming `build_pick_ledger` was `test_league_view_wiring`, and it asserts the literal
STRING `"pick_ledger = build_pick_ledger(snapshot)"` appears once in a source block. **That is a
wiring assertion — it never calls the function.** So a function at three call sites, producing
what a documentation review called *"the single dynasty fact the product most needs"*, could have
returned anything at all and the suite would have stayed green.

Lifting is what made the gap visible: a function inside a 5,800-line Streamlit hull is hard to
call, and a module is not. `test_pick_ledger.py` — 9 tests — now pins the behaviour:

| arm | failures | what it defends |
|---|---|---|
| unmutated | 0 | — |
| drop the `original == current` skip | **2** | an untouched pick is not an entry |
| `is None` → falsiness | **1** | **roster 0 is a real roster**, not a missing value |
| record only the acquiring side | **5** | one `traded_picks` row is TWO facts |
| store ids instead of the vendor row | **2** | callers price these; season and round must survive |

The falsiness arm is the one worth keeping: `if not original` would have silently dropped every
pick belonging to roster `0`, and nothing would have failed.

### Verified

```
function body byte-identical to app.py's: True
test_pick_ledger 9 tests OK; test_league_view_wiring + test_api_surface 41 tests OK
all seven ratchets PASS; floors 243 modules / 7633 assertions
```

## `#312` — ONE PALETTE AT LAST, AND IT TURNED OUT TO HAVE THREE HOMES

`design_system.TOKENS` adopts the prototype's 27 shared values. Owner ruled the direction.
Afterwards: **27 shared names, 0 disagreeing.** `status-ok` and `status-bad` keep this file's
values because the prototype does not define them.

### Why this stopped being cosmetic

Four defects in one session traced to the two homes, and **not one looked like a palette problem
when it was found**:

| item | how it presented |
|---|---|
| `#321` | `#318`'s reserved-hue rule bound on ONE of three pills — breaches measured in one home, rule written over the other |
| `#324` | a WCAG comment whose contrast figures matched no ground this repo defines; closest match was the OTHER palette's border token |
| `#327` | a divergence table `#320` had already made vacuous |
| (mine) | two different WR contrast numbers in consecutive commands, half an hour after writing the rule about exactly this |

`#321`'s two-home loop now ranges over one home twice and **stays as written**: a trivially-true
rule costs nothing, and deleting it would have to be undone the next time a value is spelled twice.

### FINDING: THERE WAS A THIRD HOME

`.streamlit/config.toml` spells seven hexes that must be `TOKENS` values verbatim. The two-home
analysis that drove this whole thread never mentioned it. It cannot import Python — Streamlit
reads it at startup — so a literal file plus `#173`'s test is the right mechanism, and **that
test is what caught it**, failing 11 subtests the moment the tokens moved.

Remapped by **token identity**, not by eye: each hex was resolved to the token name it held in
the committed `design_system.py`, then rewritten to that same token's new value. `bg -> bg`,
`gold -> gold`. Matching by appearance would have been the `#313` error again.

### FINDING: MY PRE-FLIGHT WAS THE WRONG INSTRUMENT, TWICE

I hand-wrote a pre-flight that simulated adoption against **the four rules I knew about**, and it
reported all four PASS. Applying the change produced **14 failures**. The cheapest complete
pre-flight — running `test_design_system` against a mutated palette — was available the whole time
and would have found all of them. I checked the population I could remember instead of the one
the suite already encodes.

It also had a **method hole**. It reported "absence marker vs pills: 33.61 unchanged", because
`POSITION_PILL_ABSENT = TOKENS["muted"]` is DERIVED AT IMPORT: simulating a new token table does
not move a constant that was already resolved. The real post-adoption value is **31.80**. Both
clear 25.0, so the conclusion survived — by luck, not by method.

### Nearly corrected two sentences that were already correct

`:70` says the repaint took the worst accent pair "16.4 -> 35.2", and today's worst pair is 25.8.
That looked like a fourth stale-prose instance. It is not: `:86`, three lines below, records that
amber was added LATER and "was squeezed -- dE 25.8 from gold and 26.2 from block, **against 35.2
for every other pair**". Both sentences are past-tense and scoped to events, and read together
they are exactly right. **A number that does not match today is not stale if it is scoped to an
event** — the mirror of `#319b`'s lesson, and the reflex built up over this session would have
"fixed" both.

### THE COST, recorded rather than hidden

| pair | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| eight-accent worst | 25.8 (gold/amber) | **23.9 (amber/block)** |
| `amber-b` vs `block-b` | 23.8 | **20.5** |

Nothing breaks: the ACCENT tokens are deliberately unfloored (`test_design_system.py:350` records
that a floor there "would fail five of the six existing pills"), and all four enforced rules still
clear 25.0 — reserved-hue **27.85**, injury **29.51**, quiet-text **31.80**, absence **31.80**.
The separation is genuinely smaller. The deciding argument is that these are the values that
**actually render on the surface being promoted**; this file's were the ones nobody had ever seen
in a render.

### `TokenRgbaTests` were a third-order palette home

Three tests spelled triplets by hand — `assertEqual(ds.token_rgba("emerald", 0.18),
"rgba(26,158,75,0.18)")` — so they had memorised emerald's and crimson's hexes and broke when
those moved. Retyping the new numbers would have rebuilt the same trap. What is under test is the
CONVERSION, which is a property of the function and not of whichever colour a token holds, so the
expected triplet is now derived independently from the token's own hex. The FORMAT stays pinned,
because `rgba(26,158,75,0.18)` with no spaces is what the CSS consumes.

## `#328` — 28 OF 28 MOCKUP PAGES WERE PRE-`#311`, AND THE INDEX LINKED NINE THE BUILD COULD NOT EMIT

Measured when found: **every one of the 28 pages under `mockups/` carried superseded hexes**, and
`grep -c pill-IDP mockups/index.html` returned **0** — so every page was a pre-`#311` output,
drawing DL, LB and DB in one colour and omitting IDP entirely. `mockups/common.py`'s own first
line claims this family takes *"the design tokens (from design_system, never a second copy)"*.

### Two causes, both invisible because a page that is never rebuilt never fails

**1. A second palette in SOURCE.** `c_variants.py:394` spelled

```js
const FACET = { QB: "#8f86f0", RB: "#17bfa0", WR: "#4aa8ef", TE: "#e8683f",
                K: "#a09480", DEF: "#ef7fc0", DL: "#a09480", LB: "#a09480", DB: "#a09480" };
```

by hand, so **no rebuild could repair it**. Four values superseded by `#311`/`#318`, IDP absent,
and DL/LB/DB all on the old K neutral — re-implementing in code the exact defect `#311` was
raised to end. Both call sites fell back to **`FACET.K`, the KICKER's real colour**: the same
hole `#325` closed in the prototype's `pc()`, in its second home. Now emitted by
`common.facet_js()` from `design_system`, with `ABSENT` alongside the ten so a caller has a real
fallback to name.

**2. The index advertised nine pages the build could not regenerate.** `build.py:89` looped over
`r_variants.VARIANTS + s_variants.VARIANTS` only, while `index_html()` put
`cards(c_variants.VARIANTS)` and `cards(b_variants.VARIANTS)` straight into the index. No
recorded reason for the asymmetry, no other module writing them, and all nine were **~117 lines
behind their own generator** — still carrying the pre-`#311`/`#318` pills AND the pre-`#312`
tokens.

**The regeneration was checked before it was done**, not after: all nine were generated to a
scratch directory and diffed against the committed versions first. The entire diff is the token
block, the derived badge CSS and the spec card `common.page()` builds — nothing hand-authored was
at risk. That check is the only reason it was safe to change the emit loop rather than record the
asymmetry and stop.

**3. A dead loop, the `#322` shape again.** `common.py:119-121` re-emitted `.pill-DL/LB/DB` after
the loop above it already had — dead since `#311` widened the dict to ten, and invisible because
a duplicate CSS rule with identical content changes nothing on screen.

### Result

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| pages carrying superseded hexes | **28 of 28** | **2** |
| `pill-IDP` in `index.html` | 0 | 1 |

The remaining two — `draft_rail.html` and `draft_room_compass.html` — are hand-written, emitted
by no builder, **linked from neither `index.html` nor any other page**, and referenced only by
`DRAFT_ROOM_UI.md`. Hand-editing them to today's palette would be editing a record to make a test
green, which is the move `#323` declined for `_v1_ledger_rail_prev.html`. They are exempted by a
**count-pinned** set, and the test fails if that set grows or if a name in it stops existing.

### The guard, which is the actual deliverable

`#320` built an emitter for the prototype with no check on its OUTPUT, and a stale build slipped
through within the hour (`#324`). Here the emitter and its output side ship together.
`test_mockups_palette.py`, 4 tests:

| arm | failures | what it defends |
|---|---|---|
| unmutated | 0 | — |
| `pill_css` returns the pre-`#312` CSS | **26** | every pill-carrying page, i.e. a stale build |
| `facet_js` returns the hand-written dict | **1** | the source-level second palette |
| restore the dead DL/LB/DB loop | **1** | `pill_css` emits exactly one rule per position |
| empty the exemption set | **1** | the count pin is load-bearing |
| restore the `FACET.K` fallback | **1** | `#325`'s hole, in its second home |

```
82 targeted tests across 4 modules: OK      all seven ratchets PASS
```

### THE REBUILD ALSO CAUGHT UP A CONTRACT FIELD, AND `density.json` IS HOW I FOUND OUT

`mockups/density.json` — a MEASURED artifact, written by `smoke.py` — moved on **all 16** of its
records. Fifteen moved by 1-2px; `synthesis_h3_deck.html` moved **-19px** on both `boardTop`
(255 → 236) and `pageHeight` (1436 → 1417).

A 19px shift is not a palette change, and I was one command away from committing 50 files under a
heading that said it was. Checked rather than assumed:

1. **Deterministic?** Re-ran `smoke.py`: the second run reproduced the numbers exactly. So it is
   not instrument jitter.
2. **What actually differs in the page?** Filtering the diff of every colour and token line left
   exactly one changed line: `const PAYLOAD = {...}`.
3. **What in the payload?** Diffed the two payloads field by field: **one** field differs.
   `contract.intervening_picks` was ABSENT in the committed page and is PRESENT now
   (`{"label": "Picks Until Your Next Turn", ...}`).

So these pages predate a display-contract entry, not just a palette. Rendering it reflows the deck
layout by 19px and the others by 1-2px. **This is catch-up and an improvement** — the contract is
now complete on the page — but it is a different kind of change from the one this item is named
for, and filing it silently under "palette" would have been the `#313` error in a new costume.

The density numbers are committed with their cause named, because the alternative — leaving a
measured artifact stale after running the instrument that writes it — is the defect `#323` exists
to prevent, one directory over.

## `#305` CLOSED — THE SUITE'S ONE STANDING FAILURE, FIXED WITHOUT INVENTING A MAGNITUDE

`#305` was left open deliberately, with three options and **no recommendation**, because `#56`
forbids sizing a repair to its sample and none of the three avoided that. Owner delegated the
choice. **There is a fourth option, and it needs no magnitude at all.**

### What the three options cost

| option | the problem with it |
|---|---|
| 1. bound the move against the undamped move (`move < undamped / 2`) | the `/ 2` is still a magnitude nobody argued for |
| 2. delete the test, lean on the sibling | loses the end-to-end consequence, which is what this class's docstring is about |
| 3. raise the constant to 3.5 and date it | `#56` exactly: stale again on the next reweighting, with nothing saying so |

### The fourth option: two real pools, not a toggled constant

The damping law is `base * recency * min(1.0, pool / MIN)`. **Two legitimate production states
bracket it**: a pool of 1 (factor `1/MIN`) and a pool of MIN (factor `1.0`). Comparing them IS
the ablation — at pool MIN the damping is inert, so the trusted move is the undamped move — but
performed with two REAL pools rather than by toggling a production constant, which is what `#222`
asks for.

Measured:

```
            pool   percentile   weight     law base*rec*min(1,pool/MIN)   move
thin           1        100.0   0.025000   0.025000                      3.4000
trusted       20        100.0   0.500000   0.500000                     36.5000

weight ratio trusted/thin = 20.0000   <- exactly COMPOSITE_MIN_TRUSTED_POOL_SIZE
move   ratio              = 10.7353
```

Three assertions, **none of them a magnitude anybody had to invent**:

1. **The law at pool 1, exactly** — `weight == base * recency / MIN`. The sibling test already
   pins the other end (pool == MIN, where `min()` returns 1.0); this pins the damped end in the
   same terms, from the same constants.
2. **The ratio of two PRODUCTION weights is exactly MIN** — observed off real components, not
   reconstructed. This is the assertion that catches damping being WEAKENED rather than removed.
3. **The end-to-end consequence, as an ORDERING** — `thin_move < trusted_move`. No magnitude is
   possible in an ordering. Non-vacuous because with damping removed the two weights are equal,
   both percentiles are already 100, and the two moves collapse onto each other.

The **move ratio (10.74) is recorded as an observation and deliberately NOT asserted** — it
depends on the other sources' weight mix and would rot on any reweighting. `#326`'s lesson applied
at the moment of writing rather than a year later.

### Mutation arms — the point of the whole item

| arm | result |
|---|---|
| unmutated | silent |
| damping removed (`return 1.0`) | **FIRES** |
| damping halved (divisor `MIN / 2`) | **FIRES** |
| damping softened to `sqrt(pool / MIN)` | **FIRES** |

The halved and sqrt arms are the ones the old test could never have caught.

### THE REJECTED PROSE BOUND, PROVEN VACUOUS BY MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN ARGUMENT

```
gap (naive 100th pct - draftsharks reading)  = 75.0
the prose's bound  0.5 * gap                 = 37.5
move AS SHIPPED (damping on)                 =  3.4000
move WITH DAMPING REMOVED                    = 36.5000   <- the bug restored
would assertLess(move, 37.5) catch the bug?  NO -- IT PASSES WITH THE BUG RESTORED
```

`#305` asserted this; it is now demonstrated. A test written from that sentence would have
replaced a failing test with a vacuous one, which is strictly worse.

**One figure not reconciled, recorded rather than smoothed over.** `#305` measured the undamped
move as **36.3** by setting `COMPOSITE_MIN_TRUSTED_POOL_SIZE = 1`; this pass measures **36.5** by
replacing the damping factor with `1.0`. The second ablation is narrower — it cannot disturb
anything else that reads the constant, though a grep confirms only the law does. Both land on the
same side of both bounds and the conclusion is identical, so the 0.2 is noted and not chased.

### Consequence

**The suite has no standing failure for the first time in this register's recent history.** Every
previous certification in this session reads `FAILED (failures=1 ...)` with this test named.
`data_merger.py` is unchanged — the engine's behaviour was never in doubt, and `#305` said so.

### `#305b` — AN ADVERSARIAL PASS FOUND A HOLE IN THE LIMB I HAD JUST PUSHED, AND A FUSE UNDER ALL THREE OPTIONS

Commissioned an independent in-a-vacuum review of the `#305` fix. It found two things measurement
then confirmed, and one thing measurement corrected.

**THE HOLE.** Limb 3 was a bare ordering, `assertLess(thin_move, trusted_move)`. That is just
monotonicity of a weighted mean. Measured against the mutants:

| mutation | odds ratio | bare ordering |
|---|---|---|
| unmutated | 19.9649 | pass |
| damping removed | 1.0000 | fails |
| **divisor halved** | **9.9910** | **PASSES** |
| divisor 1.0001 | 1.0000 | fails |

The weight limbs do catch a halved divisor, so the TEST was never wrong — but the only
**consequence** limb was blind to a weakening, which is half the space this class defends.

**THE REPLACEMENT, and why it survives what killed the closed form.** Adding one component at
percentile 100 and weight `w` to a mean of total weight `W` gives `(B*W + 100w)/(W + w)`, so
`move / (gap - move) == w / W` exactly. Taken at both pools, `W` CANCELS and the ratio is
`w_trusted / w_thin == MIN`. It recovers the pool factor from the SCORES while pinning only the
SHAPE of the aggregation, not the weights — which is precisely the property the rejected
closed-form candidate lacked. (It would need rewriting if the aggregator stopped being a weighted
arithmetic mean over percentiles; said in the docstring so that is a decision, not a surprise.)

The tolerance is `delta=1.0`, and it is **derived, not invented**: `score` is `round(score, 1)`,
so each of three scores carries ±0.05; propagated through the ratio that is a band of
**19.3558..20.6110**, worst deviation 0.6442. The nearest mutant sits 10.009 away, so any
tolerance in (0.64, 10.0) separates law from mutant. 1.0 is the rounding bound rounded up.

**THE FUSE — the finding that reframes the whole item.** `w_ds = 1.3 * recency(source_date)`, and
the Draft Sharks baseline is a COMMITTED fixed-date file (`2026-08-19`) decaying against
`date.today()`. It is 78 days old. So `thin_move = gap * w_b / (W + w_b)` **rises without bound as
the repository ages**:

```
   age        W  thin_move   trusted   opt3 <3.5   opt1 <und/2   ODDS RATIO
    78   0.5280     3.3908   36.4799        PASS          PASS      20.0000
   108   0.3733     4.7072   42.9392        FAIL          PASS      20.0000
   168   0.1867     8.8584   54.6119        FAIL          PASS      20.0000
   443   0.0078    57.1883   73.8499        FAIL          FAIL      20.0000
   808   0.0001    74.6571   74.9828        FAIL          FAIL      20.0000
```

**The old `3.0` was stale BY CONSTRUCTION, not mis-sized.** No value would have survived: option 3
breaks in about 30 days, and option 1 — the one that looked derived — breaks in about a year. Only
the ratio is invariant, because `W` cancels out of it. That is the measured answer to a question
`#56` could only pose: the magnitude nobody could argue for did not exist, and the reason is that
**no absolute score-delta can live in a test whose baseline decays against wall-clock time.**

**WHERE THE REVIEW WAS WRONG.** It predicted the bare ordering would PASS under a divisor of
1.0001. It FAILS — `round(score, 1)` collapses both moves onto the same reported value, so the
strict `<` does not hold. The review reasoned on unrounded values. Recorded because an adversarial
pass is evidence to check, not an oracle: four of its claims verified, one did not.

Mutation arms after the change: unmutated silent; damping removed, divisor halved, sqrt softening
and near-identity all FIRE. Ratchets all PASS, floors 244 modules / 7653 assertions.

## `#329` — THE OWNER'S THIRD COHERENCE POPULATION, MEASURED AND GUARDED

`#310` agreed this one and deferred it: *"it needs the state vocabulary to have one home across
Python and JS first."* `#311`'s entry then corrected that — the census can be written against the
divergence as it stands, and the one home is the work, not the prerequisite. This builds it.

The claim the population wants is **the same semantic state means the same thing on every
surface**. Measured, that claim is **false today**, and this file says so with numbers rather
than asserting it:

| surface | declared in | words |
|---|---|---|
| draft room | `shared.js` `KIND` | `count` `measured` `not_charged` `not_priced` `unmeasured` `withheld` (6) |
| front page | `build_front.stamp_kind` | `absent` `constructed` `measured` (3) |
| engine | `basis_semantics` | `bounded_by_rule` `bounded_input` (2) |

Three consequences, each a different defect:

1. **The two user-facing surfaces share `measured`, and nothing else.** The room can say five
   things the front page cannot express.
2. **The front page can say `constructed`** — the word that marks a figure as FABRICATED FOR A
   DEMO — **and the draft room has no way to say it at all.** That is `#187`'s most load-bearing
   word missing from the product's reference surface.
3. `basis_semantics` separates "more evidence would sharpen this" from "this is the limit of what
   is knowable", and **neither user-facing surface can render either**. The engine computes an
   epistemic distinction that never reaches a person.

### Why a ratchet and not an invariant

Registering this in `invariant_registry` today would mean registering a census against a claim the
code contradicts. `boundary_census` is the model: it allows the reaches that exist and watches for
one more while the work to get to zero proceeds. So this allows three vocabularies and fails on a
fourth, and the number falling is the repair landing.

### WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT ASSERT, and the test that keeps it that way

The divergence itself. `room_only` is 5 and `front_only` is 2 — and **a repair makes those fall**,
so pinning today's numbers would make the repair fail the test. That is how a census stops being a
ratchet and becomes a cast.

`test_a_repair_does_not_fail_the_ratchet` exists to prevent exactly that: it simulates the draft
room gaining `constructed`, asserts the shared set rises to two, and asserts the ratchet stays
GREEN. A guard that fires on an improvement is the inverted instrument this register has already
caught twice (`_python_rendered_figure_sites`, and `#311`'s own quiet-text rule).

What it DOES guard, in two separate directions:

- a **fourth** vocabulary — another home the words must be kept in step across by hand
- the shared set **shrinking** below 1 — at zero, no semantic state would mean the same thing on
  both user-facing surfaces, which is this population failing outright rather than partially

### The words are DERIVED, and that was tested the hard way

Each surface carries a reader, so the words come out of its own declaration. `shared.js` moved
three times today (`#316`, `#320`, `#325`) and the readers still resolve — which is the whole
argument for deriving rather than listing. Two tests cover the failure mode that matters: a moved
declaration and an unreadable one both **raise**, rather than quietly reporting that a surface has
no states. A census that under-reports its own population is `#298`'s and `#222`'s shape exactly —
not a crash, a plausible report about something else.

### What it does not claim

It counts DECLARED vocabularies — a map or dispatch whose members are state words. A surface that
spells one state word inline, with no map, is invisible here, exactly as
`_surfaces_consulting_the_withholding_policy` cannot see a surface that never asks. That is what
the per-surface rendering tests are for; this counts the sources of truth.

### Verified

```
9 tests OK;  state_vocabulary --check PASS
all EIGHT ratchets PASS (this is the eighth)
floors 245 modules / 7667 assertions
```

## `#331` — FOUR RULINGS, AND THE FREEZE GATE GETS A DEFINITION INSTEAD OF AN INTENTION

Owner answered four open questions. Recorded here because three of them close items that were
explicitly left open for exactly this, and one of them changes what a document is FOR.

| question | ruling |
|---|---|
| next build | **the front page** (`MAIN_PAGE.md`) |
| v4-freeze | **engine stays OPEN for now** — but a new wave of engine modifications demands a freeze down the road for base production level; pencil one in, battery/suite/adversarial passes all included |
| `DRAFT_ROOM_UI.md:50` and the mock Debate button | **mock stays ungated**, exemption recorded explicitly |
| `#329`'s state-vocabulary divergence | **the draft room gains `constructed`** |

### `#317b` — the mock exemption is now a RULING, not an inference

`#317` gated the live Debate button and flagged the problem honestly: `DRAFT_ROOM_UI.md:50` says
*"Debate is callable only while on the clock"*, full stop, and reading an unqualified rule
narrowly is what this register forbids. So the narrowing was put to the owner rather than
committed.

Ruled: the mock button (`app.py:5257`) is exempt. **The reason matters more than the ruling** —
in a mock draft the user drives every pick, so they are always on the clock; the gate could never
fire and would be decorative while still costing a branch to read. Both buttons spend the same
three provider calls, so this is a deliberate cost decision rather than an oversight. Written into
`DRAFT_ROOM_UI.md:50` itself, where the rule lives, not only here.

### The freeze gate: a DEFINITION, not a date

The owner's phrasing — *"pencil one in for later, battery/suite/adversarial passes all
included"* — asks for a gate that can be RUN, not an intention that can drift. So
`FREEZE_CHECKLIST.md` now carries the gate's definition: all three passes, on one commit, plus
the eight ratchets and the render gate where a prototype asset moved.

**That changes what that file is for, deliberately.** It was SUPERSEDED as a STATE SNAPSHOT
because six documents pointed there for "the current state" and the target went stale — `#313`'s
finding that a pointer is only as good as its target's maintenance. Current state still lives in
this register's tail and that pointer stands. What lives there now is a PROCEDURE, which cannot
go stale the same way: it is wrong only if the procedure changes, and then it is wrong loudly.

Three failure modes are written into the gate because this repository has hit all three:

1. a multi-hour battery reclaimed 13 minutes in, losing everything but one arm, because CPU does
   not count as session activity
2. `requirements.txt`'s own warning — *"a reclaimed container ran the suite 14 tests lighter and
   reported OK. A freeze must be licensed by a suite that RAN, not one that quietly stood down"*
   — so the gate checks the test COUNT against the dated table, not just the verdict
3. the adversarial pass is evidence, not an oracle: at `#305b` a commissioned review found a real
   hole AND made a claim measurement contradicted, four of five verified, and the one that failed
   verification is recorded as having failed

### What this does not do

It does not schedule the freeze, and it does not argue for one. `#305` closed having confirmed the
engine's behaviour is not in question. The gate exists to license a freeze when the owner calls
it, not to find reasons to delay it.

## `#330` — THE DRAFT ROOM GAINS `constructed`, AND THE PRODUCER WAS FOUND BEFORE THE WORD

Owner ruled at `#331` that `#329`'s divergence is repaired by the draft room gaining
`constructed`. **Acting on that literally would have shipped a dead token**, so the producer was
found first — and finding it took three attempts, two of which measurement killed.

### Why the word could not just be added

`#320` emitted an `--absent` CSS token that nothing read, and `#325` had to go back and wire it.
A vocabulary word with no producer is that defect exactly. So before touching `KIND`, every
provenance field the room's data carries was enumerated:

```
denial_basis        measured 700/700        displacement_basis  measured 700/700
depth_basis         vacant / no_surplus / measured / roster_partially_priced
replacement_basis   live_starter_demand / predraft_anchor / startable_floor / pool_truncated
availability_basis  no_designation / immaterial_designation / unrecognised_designation
risk_basis          designation_not_priced  slot_share_basis    even_flex_split
bpa_source          points_vor_sleeper_season_scored / position_relative_trade_value_vor
```

**Eight fields, and not one of them can be `constructed`.** Every value is engine-derived.

**Two hypotheses killed by measurement, recorded so nobody re-runs them:**

1. *`pick_synthesis.py` produces CONSTRUCTED.* It does not — those two hits are PROSE IN
   COMMENTS describing a SCALE that was constructed, and the second one explains that
   construction was since removed. A grep hit is not a producer.
2. *The fallback-priced candidate is constructed.* It is not. A candidate on
   `position_relative_trade_value_vor` has `projected_points: null` and `universal_value: 0.0`,
   so the room's existing `not_priced` is already correct there. The basis prose beside it is
   about `universal_value`, not about the points row.

### The real producer: the SEAT IDENTITY

The front page stamps its `team` field `CONSTRUCTED -- the seat's label in a replayed battery,
not an owner's team name`. **The draft room renders exactly that and had no way to say so**: it
writes `Roster 6` wherever a live league would write an owner's team name, from a fixture whose
`seat` is an integer 1-12.

Same fact, same word, on both surfaces now — which is the entire point of the coherence
population `#329` measures. The stamp's wording is copied from the front page's deliberately, so
the two surfaces say the same thing rather than two things that happen to rhyme.

### A scope claim I made and immediately falsified

The first version of the helper's comment said *"one home for how a seat is written"*. A grep for
the whole population falsified it on the spot: **seven sites render a seat, and the helper reached
two.** `#316` is the identical lesson — scoping to the sites already in hand and calling it
complete. The roster-card header (`M.allRosters`'s `<h4>`) was the missed identity site and is now
stamped.

The other four are **deliberately** unstamped, and the reason is the owner's standing constraint
rather than an oversight: on the pick board a seat is a COORDINATE ("who holds #67"), not a claim
about who someone is. There are 168 of them, and a tooltip on each would bury the one place the
stamp means something. A stamp repeated everywhere stops being read.

Measured after: **13 seat labels carry the stamp** (2 on the clock line, 11 roster cards — twelve
seats less "You"), console clean.

### The census moved, and the ratchet followed it

```
shared by the two user-facing surfaces: constructed, measured   (was: measured alone)
the front page can say, the room cannot : absent                (was: absent, constructed)
```

`test_a_repair_does_not_fail_the_ratchet` was written at `#329` simulating *this exact repair* and
asserting the ratchet would stay green. **It did.** The design held on its first real test.

**`SHARED_FLOOR` rises 1 -> 2.** A ratchet that does not move with its own repair is just a
ceiling: the gain would be lossless to give back, silently.

### TWO TEST ARMS WENT STALE THE MOMENT THE REPAIR LANDED, FOR `#305`'s REASON

1. `test_losing_the_one_shared_word_fails` patched `SHARED_FLOOR` to the literal `2`. That tripped
   the ratchet while the surfaces shared ONE word and **silently stopped tripping it** the moment
   they shared two. Now derived: `len(shared) + 1`, an arm that cannot go stale.
2. `test_a_repair_does_not_fail_the_ratchet` simulated gaining `constructed` — now simply true, so
   the simulation was moved on to the NEXT repair (`absent`), with an added assertion that
   adopting it would leave `front_only` empty and close the user-facing half of this population.

This is `#305`'s lesson arriving one day later in tests I had written the day before: **an
absolute constant in a test whose baseline moves is an arm that disarms itself.** The register has
now recorded that failure twice in two days, in two unrelated files.

### Verified

```
84 tests across 4 modules OK;  all EIGHT ratchets PASS
floors 245 modules / 7668 assertions
13 stamped seat labels, console clean, DOM verified free of stray whitespace
```

## `#332` — BOTH COMMITTED FRONT PAGES WERE PAINTED IN A PALETTE THE SYSTEM OF RECORD ABANDONED, AND 4,373 TESTS WERE GREEN

Found on the first step of the front-page marathon the owner sanctioned in `#331`, while
establishing a byte-identity baseline before refactoring. The baseline did not hold, and the
reason was worth more than the refactor.

### The measurement

```
committed ui_explore/round3/front.html        27 of 29 shared colour tokens stale
committed ui_explore/round3/front_empty.html  27 of 29 shared colour tokens stale

  --bg         #15120b -> #0c0a07        --ink        #ece3d2 -> #f2ead9
  --surface    #1f1a11 -> #17130d        --gold       #d4a017 -> #c9961a
  --emerald    #1a9e4b -> #0b8f57        --violet     #9457d4 -> #6d3fd6
  ... 21 more
```

`#312` adopted the prototype's 27 shared token values into `design_system.TOKENS` — the one home
the front page derives its colours from, by calling `root_css_block()`. Nothing rebuilt the two
committed pages. **`#312`'s headline was "one palette, 27 names 0 disagreeing", and it shipped
beside two committed artifacts painted entirely in the palette it had just abandoned.**

Left and right in that table are both correct readings of this repo at different times, which is
the whole problem: the page was right when it was built and became wrong without being touched.

### Why nothing failed

Three guards could have caught it and none was pointed at the artifact:

| guard | what it covers | why it missed |
|---|---|---|
| the 34 round-3 tests | `build_front.build()` / `build_empty.build()` | every one calls `build()` **in memory** and asserts on the returned string; not one reads the file on disk |
| the render gate | round 2's built pages, hashed | `grep round3 _shoot.py` → nothing. Checked, not assumed |
| `test_design_system` | `design_system.py`'s own values | it is the thing that CHANGED; it has no concept of a downstream artifact |

So the builders were tested and the artifacts were not. A test that rebuilds can never see
staleness, because rebuilding is the repair.

### This is `#328`'s defect in a second place

`#328` found 28 stale committed mockup pages and shipped `test_mockups_palette.py` beside the
emitter so the next drift would fail loudly. The identical shape existed one directory over and
nobody grepped for the other generator. **A guard written for one emitter is not a guard on the
practice** — the same sentence `#327` had to write about `MAIN_PAGE.md` being the second home of
a claim `#322` had already repaired. Three occurrences now, same root: a repair applied where it
was found rather than everywhere it applies.

### The repair

Both pages rebuilt, and `test_front_pages_match_their_builders.py` added at top level — **not**
beside its subject, and the reason is `#308`: `ui_explore/round3/` was invisible to the
certification suite for its whole life (34 tests that passed by hand and were never once reached
by `unittest discover`, because neither `ui_explore/` nor `ui_explore/round3/` had an
`__init__.py`). Both exist now and `#308` closed that, but a guard whose purpose is to catch an
unguarded artifact does not belong in the directory that was recently unreachable.

Two tests, table-driven so a third page arrives as one row with its guard already attached:

1. **byte-identity** — `build(fixture)` must equal the committed file exactly. `build()`, not
   `main()`: `main()` WRITES, and a check that invokes the repair can never report that the
   repair was needed.
2. **the palette, against its cause** — every colour token on a committed page must be the hex
   `design_system.TOKENS` spells today. Test 1 would also fail here but could not say why; this
   one names the quantity and keeps firing if a page is ever rebuilt from a COPY of the palette
   instead of from `root_css_block()`.

### Mutation panel — 4 arms, 11 firing subtests, and one deliberate silence

| arm | mutation | byte-identity | palette |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `front.html` → its committed state | `[front]` | `[front]` |
| 2 | `front_empty.html` → its committed state | `[empty]` | `[empty]` |
| 3 | `design_system.TOKENS["bg"]` → `#010203` | `[front] [empty]` | `[front] [empty]` |
| 4 | prose `Everything else` in `build_front.py` | `[front]` | **silent, correctly** |

Arm 4 is the one that proves the two tests are not one test twice: a change that moves the page
without touching a colour fires byte-identity alone, and only on the page that carries the string.

Also verified in a real browser, because `#324` is the standing reason not to trust text
matching about CSS: `getComputedStyle(documentElement)['--bg']` resolves to `#0c0a07` and
`body`'s background computes to `rgb(12, 10, 7)` on both pages. The palette is in EFFECT, not
merely present.

### Two corrections — both mine, both in the instrument, both while measuring this

**1. I rebuilt a committed artifact by accident and then measured my own repair.** `build_empty.py`
reads `argv[0]` as the FIXTURE path, not the output path. Invoking it with a single scratchpad
argument raised, and the `||` fallback I had written ran it with NO arguments — which writes to
the real `ui_explore/round3/front_empty.html`. The guard then reported `front_empty.html` as
current, and I briefly published that "only `front.html` is stale". **Both pages were stale.** The
reading was of a file I had just fixed without noticing. Caught by `git status` showing ` M` on a
file I had no reason to have modified.

**2. Two mutation arms were measured against a mutation still in effect.** I restored
`design_system.py` with `cp` from a backup and re-ran — and the test still read the mutated
value, because `__pycache__` held a compiled module Python trusted. Arms 2 and 3 of the first
panel were therefore void, and arm 3 appeared to prove the palette test fires on a prose change,
which would have meant the two tests were redundant. This is `#240` ("clear `__pycache__` before
measuring") arriving somewhere its own entry does not mention: **mutation testing, where the
restore is as much a measurement as the mutation.** The panel above was re-run with a cache clear
before every single probe, and `git checkout --` rather than `cp`.

**And arm 4 of that first panel proved nothing at all.** I mutated `"Nothing needs you"` — a
string that only renders when the claim band is EMPTY, and the fixture carries two claims, so it
never reaches the page. The mutation was a no-op and the silence I read as a result was the
silence of nothing having happened. A mutation that does not change the artifact is not a weak
test, it is not a test. The corrected arm greps the built page for the string first.

### EVERY line pointer in `MAIN_PAGE.md` was wrong — four of four

I started by checking the two that a CORRECTION dated 2026-11-04 had just re-pinned, found both
stale again, and then checked the other two rather than assuming they were fine. They were not:

| pointer | the doc said | measured |
|---|---|---|
| the only `st.stop()` | `app.py:3667` | **3610** |
| the five-view `st.segmented_control` | `app.py:3742` | **3685** |
| `lineup_readiness.compute_readiness` | `app.py:3886` | **3765** |
| `league_standings.team_standings` | `app.py:6200` | **6085** |

**Four of four**, two of them re-pinned forty-eight hours earlier. All corrected in place. The
figure moved because I checked the rest instead of writing up the two I had tripped over — the
difference between "two pointers went stale" and "this form does not work here" is the whole
finding, and only the second one is actionable.

A pointer that needed correcting twice in two days is not a maintenance failure, it is a FORM
failure — `#313`'s rule that a pointer is only as good as its target's
maintenance, with the durable repair being to name the symbol (`st.stop()`, `st.segmented_control`
over `MATCHUP_VIEW…IMPORT_VIEW`) and let a reader grep, rather than a line number that decays on
every edit above it. Done here; the line numbers are kept beside the names as a convenience that
is allowed to rot.

### What is NOT fixed

- **The front page still is not in the app.** It is a prototype in `ui_explore/round3/` and
  production still shows `st.title` + `st.info` + `st.stop()` at `app.py:3606-3610`. That is the
  marathon `#331` sanctioned and this item is its first step, not its delivery.
- **The claim band's judgment still has exactly one home and it is a prototype's HTML emitter.**
  `LADDER`, `CAP`, the futurity rule that ranks on the worst week STILL AHEAD, the within-rung
  ordering and all four rung conditions live inside `build_front.build()`, interleaved with
  f-strings. Production cannot reach any of it without re-implementing it, which `#126` forbids.
  This is the same shape `#297` fixed for `positional_depth`, and `MAIN_PAGE.md` already named it
  the honest first cost of this page. **It is the next item, and it was what I set out to do
  before the baseline failed to hold.**

### CERTIFICATION — `#332`

```

OK (skipped=2, expected failures=1)

eight ratchets green   assertion_floors: no guarantee has shrunk (246 modules held to a floor)
```

4373 → **4375**: the two tests this item adds. Fourth consecutive green suite.

| commit | tests | seconds | ms/test | verdict |

| `ef6a07d` | 4364 | 1401.862 | 321.2 | OK |
| `bfc2420` | 4373 | 1409.280 | 322.2 | OK |

306.6 ms/test is the fastest per-test figure recorded, on the largest suite recorded. Budget from
the worst recent total: **1508s**.

**The render gate was NOT run for this item, and that is a reasoned omission rather than a skip.**

## `#333` — THE FRONT PAGE'S JUDGMENT HAD ONE HOME AND IT WAS A PROTOTYPE'S HTML EMITTER

`MAIN_PAGE.md` named this the honest first cost of the page, ahead of any layout, and it was
right. Every ruling the claim band makes — the ladder, the cap, the futurity rule, the within-rung
ordering and all four rung conditions — was spelled inside `ui_explore/round3/build_front.build()`,
interleaved with the f-strings that draw the HTML. One caller could reach it: a prototype that
emits a static file.

So production had two options and both were forbidden. Re-implement the ranking in `app.py` — a
second source of truth, which `#126` forbids. Or text-extract it from the builder — which is what
`test_positional_depth_coverage` had to do before `#297` lifted `positional_depth` out of
`app.py`, and which that item recorded as a workaround, named as one.

**This is `#297`'s lift in the opposite direction.** `#297` moved a quantity OUT of the one module
nothing can import. This moves a judgment OUT of the one module only a prototype calls.

### What moved, and what deliberately did not

`front_claims.py` carries `LADDER`, `CAP`, `byes_ahead`, `thin_sort_key` and `compose`, and
contains **no HTML**. A claim is measured values plus the basis flags that qualify them — never a
sentence.

The prose stayed in the builder, and that is a ruling rather than laziness. Two surfaces say the
same thing differently: a static page writes *"1 of your starters sits that week"*; Streamlit may
not. A module that shipped copy would make the page's voice something production had to override
instead of write. Same rule `depth_ratings` follows — the engine returns the label, the surface
writes the sentence.

### The proof, which only existed because `#332` ran first

Rebuilding `front.html` through the rewired builder reproduces the committed file's **sha256
exactly**:

```
7e78424f0d8d342c9f1e5a224df5c78bd321562858d9f3c6b7420b68a3bbbe80   rewired build
7e78424f0d8d427f...                                                  (identical)
```

That check is the only reason a refactor of a certified artifact is safe to make at all — and it
is the check `#332` found broken the day before, with both committed pages painted in a palette
`design_system` had abandoned. **Doing this lift first would have had no baseline to stand on, and
nothing would have said so**: the comparison would have "passed" against a file that was already
wrong, or failed for a reason that had nothing to do with the refactor. The ordering was luck, not
planning, and it is worth recording as the reason to establish a baseline before trusting one.

Also verified: all 18 existing tests in `test_front_renders_its_basis` — the RENDERING contract —
pass unchanged against the rewired builder, confirmed loaded from the rewired copy rather than the
original.

### The clock rung is declared and has never fired

Pinned while lifting, because it was invisible until the rungs were listed in one place:
`"clock"` is the ladder's top rung — the only one carrying a deadline a reader can actually miss —
and **nothing produces it.** No fixture key supplies it; no branch emits it. So the band's
ordering has only ever been exercised on three of its four rungs.

That is a known absence, not dead code to delete: when the app knows you are on the clock, that
claim should outrank everything, and the ladder already says so. `RUNGS_PRODUCED_HERE` pins the
gap, and a test asserts the two lists disagree in exactly this way — so wiring the draft clock
later has to come past that test rather than quietly satisfy it.

### What is NOT fixed

**The front page still is not in the app.** `front_claims` is now reachable by production and
unreached by it. `app.py:3606-3610` is still `st.title` + `st.info` + `st.stop()`. That is the
next item and the actual delivery of the marathon `#331` sanctioned; this is the prerequisite it
could not be built without.

### Mutation panel — 9 arms

| arm | tests fired |
|---|---|
| baseline | **0** |
| ladder: the `hole` rung renamed | 7 |
| `CAP` 3 → 4 | 1 |
| futurity: `>= now` becomes `> now` | 3 |
| futurity: `current_week` ignored entirely | 3 |
| thin ordering: count dropped from the sort key | 1 |
| `priced_floor` always False | 1 |
| `concentration`: None coerced to 0 | 1 |
| `clock` added to `RUNGS_PRODUCED_HERE` | 1 |
| holes: one claim per hole instead of one card | 1 |
| restored | **0** |

### Two instrument failures, and the second one found a real defect

**1. The first panel was entirely void, and it took the file's own status to see it.**
`git checkout -- front_claims.py` fails on an UNTRACKED file — `pathspec did not match any
file(s) known to git` — and the new module had not been committed yet. So nothing was ever
restored and the nine mutations ACCUMULATED, each reading reporting every previous arm's damage
as well as its own. The failure counts rose monotonically down the list, which is the tell.

This is the **second restore failure in this session**, with a different mechanism each time.
`#332`'s was a `cp` restore shadowed by a `__pycache__` Python trusted; this one was a restore
command that printed an error and returned non-zero while the loop carried on. The general rule
both of them point at: **a restore is a measurement and gets the same scepticism as the
mutation.** The corrected panel copies from a pristine source and `cmp`s after every single arm,
so a restore that does not restore stops the run instead of silently poisoning the next nine
readings.

**2. The void panel still found something, and it was a test that tested nothing.**
One arm — dropping the count from `thin_sort_key`, i.e. reverting to the alphabetical ordering
the key exists to prevent — added **no new failing test**, visible even through the accumulation
because every other arm did. The cause:

```
the test's fixture  TE(2), QB(1)  ->  by count ['QB','TE']   by alphabet ['QB','TE']   same
a fixture that works QB(2), TE(1)  ->  by count ['TE','QB']   by alphabet ['QB','TE']   differ
```

`test_thin_positions_rank_by_how_empty_the_room_is_not_by_the_alphabet` asserted `["QB","TE"]`
against a fixture where **ranking by count and ranking alphabetically give the same answer**. It
asserted the right answer for the wrong reason and passed against either implementation. Fixed to
QB(2)/TE(1), where only one ordering can pass; the arm now fires.

The irony is exact and worth keeping: this is `#332`'s arm-4 error one level up. There, a
*mutation* that could not change the artifact proved nothing. Here, a *test* whose fixture could
not distinguish the behaviours proved nothing — and it had been copied forward from the original
code's own comment, which cites a real league where the thin position happened to be QB, the
alphabetically-first code. **A real-world example is not automatically a discriminating one.**

### A THIRD instrument failure, in the close-out procedure itself

Caught only because a stop hook kept asking for a commit and I went to establish why waiting was
correct. **Two of the eight ratchets enumerate via `git ls-files`, and a new file is invisible to
them until it is staged.**

```
assertion_floors  boundary_census  skip_gates  suite_reach  api_surface  state_vocabulary   filesystem
doc_index  prose_names                                                                      GIT LS-FILES
```

`prose_names` scans tracked `*.py` at four separate call sites — it reads every backticked name
inside each module's prose and requires it to resolve. `front_claims.py` and
`test_front_claims.py` were UNTRACKED when I ran the ratchets, so **`prose_names --check` passed
without ever opening either new file.** It was a green reading of a tree that did not contain the
work. `doc_index` is scoped to `*.md` and was unaffected, and the other six scan the filesystem
and did see the new modules — so six of eight readings were valid and two were vacuous.

The ordering in `close-register-item` puts the ratchets after the suite and before the commit,
which is the wrong order for any item that ADDS a file: at that point the file is still untracked
and the two index-reading ratchets cannot see it. **The order that measures what is actually
being committed is `git add` FIRST, then the ratchets, then the suite.** Re-run against the
staged tree, all eight are green — but that is a different measurement from the one I had, and
only the second one means anything.

This is the session's third instrument failure and they rhyme: a `__pycache__` that shadowed a
restore, a `git checkout` that could not restore an untracked file, and now two ratchets that
could not see an untracked file. All three are the same question answered wrong — **what is the
instrument actually looking at** — and in each case the reading was green, plausible, and about
something else.

### `#333b` — THE SUITE FAILED, AND THE FAILURE WAS THE BEST EVIDENCE THE LIFT WORKED

The certification run came back `FAILED (failures=1)`:

```
FAIL: test_quantity_readers.TheWriteOnlySetMustNotGrowTests
      .test_a_write_only_quantity_that_gained_a_reader_is_noticed
AssertionError: ['concentration', 'starters_out'] != []
  : these are no longer write-only. Good -- remove them from KNOWN_WRITE_ONLY and
    note which commit gave them a reader.
```

That is `#138`'s write-only scanner, reconciled in both directions, firing in the **good** one.
Two engine quantities that nothing in production read now have a reader.

**And the mechanism is the independent witness this refactor could not have produced for itself.**
`quantity_readers`'s surface set is the top-level `*.py` files plus a closed module list. Both
quantities were already read by the front-page prototype — but a read inside
`ui_explore/round3/build_front.py` was never a read by production, and the scanner was right to
say so. Lifting the claim band into top-level `front_claims.py` is what moved them from
`write_only` to `carried`. So the claim "`#333` makes this judgment reachable by production" was
checked by an instrument with no part in the refactor and no knowledge of it, and it agreed.

Observed from the scanner rather than reasoned about:

```
concentration     write_only=False   verdict=carried
starters_out      write_only=False   verdict=carried
worst_week_loss   write_only=True    verdict=write_only
```

**`worst_week_loss` did not resolve, and that is reported rather than explained away.**
`front_claims` references it; the scanner still grades it write-only. `#222`'s rule is to observe
the production quantity and never overrule the instrument with a reconstruction — and overruling
a correct instrument on a recomputed number is an error already made once this session, on a
token count. Why this one differs from the two above is **unmeasured**, and saying so is more
useful than a guess that would read like a finding.

Repair: both removed from `KNOWN_WRITE_ONLY` with the commit that gave them a reader recorded
beside them. Both directions re-checked — restoring `concentration` fires the gained-a-reader
arm; dropping a still-write-only `players_out` fires the no-new-write-only arm.

**A fourth restore failure, same session, fourth mechanism.** Mutation arm A used
`git checkout -- test_quantity_readers.py`, which succeeded — and reverted the file to HEAD,
discarding the uncommitted repair rather than the mutation. The `cmp` that the earlier failures
had taught me to add is the only reason it was caught. The file was tracked (unlike `#333`'s
case) and the command returned zero (unlike `#333`'s case), so neither previous lesson covered
it. **The general form, finally stated properly: an uncommitted change means `git checkout` is
not an undo, it is a discard.** Restore from a pristine copy taken immediately before the
mutation, and verify with `cmp` every time.

```
OK (skipped=2, expected failures=1)

front.html / front_empty.html rebuilt byte-identical -- they do not appear in `git status`
```

## `#334` — THE FRONT PAGE IS IN THE APP

The marathon `#331` sanctioned, delivered. `app.py`'s empty state was `st.title` plus one
`st.info` line, and it is the ONLY thing a person sees before syncing — the view picker is
seventy-five lines below the `st.stop()`, so every other surface is unreachable from there. One
sentence telling them to sync answers "what do I do" and nothing else: not whether the data
already on the machine is any good, not what is missing, not what syncing buys.

### The third lift in the same family, and the pattern is now explicit

```
`#297`   positional_depth   OUT of `app.py`, the one module nothing can import
`#333`   the claim band     OUT of a prototype's HTML emitter
`#334`   the have/on_sync split   OUT of a prototype's FIXTURE GENERATOR
```

Each time, a production judgment had exactly one home and that home was unreachable by
production. `front_page.compose_unsynced` is the split's home now, with **no Streamlit import in
it** — `app.py` writes the sentences, the module returns the values and the basis flags that
qualify them. That is `#333`'s ruling applied again, and here it has a second payoff: a module
that imported Streamlit could not be called by the capture script, so the fixture and production
would have drifted into two compositions of one thing — the `#126` defect all three lifts close.

`reason_of` gained one home in the same move. It was `build_front.reason_of`, reachable only by
the prototypes, and `app.py` needed the identical parse rule to strip an `ABSENT --` stamp. A
second spelling in `app.py` would have been `#126` in miniature — the kind that rots quietly
because both copies look obviously correct. `build_front` imports it from `front_page` now.

### The proof, built to not go stale

The composition is a **pure function of the manifest rows**, not of the clock or the disk. That
is deliberate: the real ages move every day, so a test that called `build_freshness_manifest` and
compared against committed numbers would be stale tomorrow BY CONSTRUCTION — `#305`'s defect
exactly, where a bound was wrong the day after it was written because the thing it bounded decays
against `date.today()`. Feeding the composition the rows implied by the committed fixture tests
the judgment and nothing else, and it reproduces that fixture **exactly**.

Both built pages also rebuild byte-identical through the `reason_of` move — they do not appear in
`git status` at all. That is `#332`'s guard earning its place a second time in two items.

### It was run, and looked at

Not a prototype claim. Streamlit 1.66.1 is installed in this container, so `app.py` was served
and screenshotted:

```
Fantasy Football Command Center
⚠️ Aging          Oldest input on disk is 79 days old.
On disk now       Draft Sharks Dynasty Rankings — 74d, as of 2026-08-25
                  Draft Sharks Trade Value Chart — 79d, as of 2026-08-20
Arrives when you sync
                  Sleeper player database — never fetched on this machine
                  Sleeper season projections (the league-scored board) — never fetched
Sync a Sleeper username in the sidebar
console errors: none
```

**79 days, where the committed fixture says 76.** That difference is the point: the page is
reading the live manifest, not the prototype's fixture.

### Looking at it found a defect reading the diff would not have

The running app showed the freshness grade **twice** — `⚠️ Aging` on the page and
`⚠️ Data Freshness: Aging` in the sidebar — two copies of one judgment on one screen. I
introduced it by wiring the front page, and it is precisely what the standing constraint on this
project names: *"clean dissemination of information over just having as much on the screen as you
can fit."*

The sidebar grade is now gated on a synced league. Unsynced, the front page carries the same
grade AND the per-source ages the sidebar caption only promises; synced, the front page is below
the stop and the sidebar is the only grade, so it stays. This is the second time this session
that **looking at a render found what text-matching could not** — `#324` found the entire
position palette dead in the browser while three string checks called it correct.

### The wiring test, and why it is weaker than it should be

`app.py` has 69 top-level Streamlit calls and no `__main__` guard, so importing it runs the
application and no test can call the empty-state branch. `test_maintenance_view_wiring` set the
precedent: read `app.py`'s SOURCE. Named as the weaker check it is — but the alternative is a
composition that is perfectly tested and reachable by nobody, which is the state `front_claims`
was in before `#333` and `positional_depth` before `#297`.

One of the three wiring assertions is an AST check that the call sits **above the only
`st.stop()`**, because a call that drifted below it would render nothing and fail no other test.

### Mutation panel — 10 arms, baseline 0, restore 0

| arm | fires |
|---|---|
| `have.sort` removed | ordering |
| worst age `max` → `min` | grade-reads-oldest, fixture anchor |
| grade hardcoded `Fresh` | grade-from-one-home, grade-reads-oldest, fixture anchor |
| no-date `worst_days` 0 instead of None | the `#187` absence arm |
| `split_reason` never splits | 4 tests incl. the fixture anchor |
| `reason_of` returns the whole stamp | 3 tests |
| `have` / `on_sync` swapped | 4 tests |
| app: sidebar gate removed | the one-grade-on-screen arm |
| app: compose call deleted | both call-exists arms |
| **app: call kept but moved BELOW the stop** | **the ordering arm alone** |

The last arm is the one that matters, and it exists because of this session's repeated lesson: a
mutation that does not exercise the specific claim proves nothing. Deleting the call fires the
"is it called" tests for the wrong reason. Moving it below the stop leaves the call present,
fires **only** `test_the_composition_is_called_ABOVE_the_only_stop`, and is therefore the only
arm that actually tests the ordering.

### A ratchet asked the question I would not have

`api_surface` failed on the first run with `UNASSIGNED MODULE: front_page -- the hull reaches it
and no layer claims it`. That is `#310`'s five-layer inventory doing exactly its job: a new module
that `app.py` imports has to declare which layer it belongs to, and the file's own rule is that
the assignment is defended by what the module says it is FOR, not by its name.

Assigned **RENDER**, on four pieces of evidence recorded beside the entry. The one that decides
it: **this module carries display COPY.** `action`, `action_cost` and every `*_basis` string is a
sentence a reader sees, and no ENGINE module does that — `freshness`, its own input, returns
`(label, as_of, days)` and nothing else. That is the line. Deriving OVER engine output does not
make a module engine when what it adds is presentation, and the have/on_sync split is a
presentation judgment that happens to be shared by two renderers, which is why it sits beside
`trade_ledger_ui` ("pure formatting/data-shaping helpers") rather than beside `freshness`.

Worth noting for the next item: `front_claims` is NOT in this inventory, because nothing in the
hull reaches it yet. The moment `app.py` imports it, this ratchet will ask the same question
about it — and the answer will be RENDER for the same reason.

### What is NOT fixed

- **The SYNCED front page is still not in the app.** `front_claims.compose` is reachable and
  unreached: the triage band — the claims, the week band, the doors — has no call site in
  production. It cannot go where this one went, because above the stop there is no roster to
  triage. Where it belongs (a sixth destination, the default landing, or something above the view
  picker) is a structural question about `app.py` and the next item.
- **The record band and the dynasty facts remain absent**, for the reasons `#306` establishes: a
  pick count derived from `league_type` and `total_rosters` is plausible, cheap, and wrong in
  exactly the case the product exists to serve.

### `#334b` — I CITED A PRECEDENT WITHOUT CHECKING HOW IT WORKED, AND THE SUITE CAUGHT IT

The certification run came back `FAILED (failures=1)`:

```
FAIL: test_ui_source.NoTestReadsAppPyDirectlyTests.test_no_test_module_reads_app_py_off_disk
AssertionError: ['test_front_page.py'] != []
  : read the UI surface through ui_source.text() instead -- an app.py read stops
    covering anything the moment a view is extracted
```

`test_front_page.py` opened `app.py` with `read_text()`, and its docstring justified that by
citing `test_maintenance_view_wiring` as precedent. **That module does read the UI source — but
through `ui_source.text()`**, which is exactly the distinction I asserted past without opening
the file. The precedent was real and I described its mechanism from memory.

The rule exists for a reason better than tidiness, and `ui_source`'s own docstring states it: an
`app.py` read stops covering anything the moment a view is extracted. `assertIn` fails loudly
then — noisy but safe. **`assertNotIn` PASSES, forever**, because the pattern genuinely is absent
from `app.py` once the code it polices moved elsewhere. A correct guard that can never execute is
the defect class this repo keeps finding.

Moved onto `ui_source`, and the ordering test got **stronger** in the process. It now scopes its
AST to the unit that actually holds the call (`ui_source.unit_containing`), because line order
across concatenated modules is an artefact of the join rather than of execution — and it asserts
the `st.stop()` is in that same unit, so a future extraction that separates them fails here
instead of silently comparing two unrelated line numbers.

### Re-running the mutation panel found a THIRD hollow test

The wiring tests changed, so their arms had to be re-run — a panel that validated the old
implementation says nothing about the new one. Arm 9, removing the import, then fired **nothing**:

```
app.py:   import front_page   ->   # import front_page
assertIn("import front_page", ui_source.text())   ->   still passes
```

Commenting an import out leaves the needle intact. The probe could not distinguish the two states
it claimed to separate, so it was not a weak test, it was not a test. Now an `ast.Import` walk
over the calling unit, which a comment cannot satisfy; the arm fires.

**Three hollow checks in three items, same shape every time:**

| item | the probe | why it proved nothing |
|---|---|---|
| `#332` | mutated `"Nothing needs you"` | that string only renders when the band is EMPTY; the fixture has two claims |
| `#333` | `TE(2), QB(1)` ordering fixture | count-order and alphabet give the same answer |
| `#334b` | `assertIn("import front_page", …)` | a commented-out import still contains the needle |

The common failure is not carelessness about mutation testing — it is the same question as the
four restore failures, one level over: **what is this probe actually able to tell apart?** A
mutation and its test are one instrument, and an instrument that cannot separate the two states
reads green in both.

### CERTIFICATION — `#334` / `#334b`

```

OK (skipped=2, expected failures=1)

eight ratchets green (api_surface now claims `front_page` as RENDER, with evidence)
both built pages rebuilt byte-identical -- absent from `git status`
the running app screenshotted: grade, two dated sources, two absent sources, one action, no console errors
```

4393 → **4410**: the 17 tests `front_page` brings. Sixth consecutive green suite.

| commit | tests | seconds | ms/test | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `f410ca9` | 4373 | 1366.836 | 312.5 | OK |
| `ce8879d` | 4375 | 1341.210 | 306.6 | OK |
| `4259a4d` | 4393 | 1377.540 | 313.6 | OK |
| **`d5739a5`** | **4410** | **1379.622** | **312.8** | **OK** |

Budget from the worst recent total: **1508s**. The suite has grown 37 tests across these four
items and the per-test cost has not moved — 306.6 to 313.6 ms, inside the run-to-run spread.

### The four items as one arc

`#331` sanctioned "the front page" as the next build. What that turned out to require, in order:

1. **`#332`** — a baseline that could be trusted. Both committed pages were painted in a palette
   the system of record had abandoned, and no guard held them. Without this, every byte-identity
   proof below would have compared against a file that was already wrong.
2. **`#333`** — the claim band's judgment out of a prototype's HTML emitter, so production could
   reach it. `test_quantity_readers` independently confirmed it by moving two engine quantities
   out of the write-only set.
3. **`#334`** — the unsynced page's split out of a prototype's fixture generator, and **into the
   app**, where it was run and looked at.
4. **`#334b`** — the suite rejecting a precedent I had cited from memory.

The ordering was not planned and `#332` was luck: I went looking for a byte-identity baseline
before refactoring and found it broken. Had the refactor gone first, its proof would have been
meaningless and nothing would have said so. **Establish the baseline before trusting it** is the
transferable part.
