## `#347` — THE LANDING PAGE IS NOT AN ANALYSIS SURFACE, AND I DREW IT AS ONE TWICE

Third attempt at this page. The first two failed the same way, and the owner named it:

> This again just feels like a rebuild of the dashboard. The landing page just needs to say
> "these leagues need attention." "resync" "add league" and the connections options, no?
> ... league management and connections/setups too, maybe
> ... as in setting up new league, deleting leagues, and the like

`#343` rebuilt the in-league dashboard. `#344` rebuilt the CLAIM BAND at twelve-league arity and
congratulated itself in its own docstring for not being a dashboard — it was still analysis,
only wider. Four of the five things the owner listed are VERBS. A page whose job is mostly verbs
is not a dashboard, and that is the distinction both earlier attempts missed.

Built at `ui_explore/round7/`: `build_landing.py`, `landing.html`, `landing_unsynced.html`,
`landing_fixture.json`, `NOTES.md`. Both pages rebuild byte-identically.

**EVERY AFFORDANCE WAS READ OUT OF `app.py` BEFORE IT WAS DRAWN.** The hard law forbids
inventing a quantity; an invented ACTION is the same defect wearing a different hat. Reading
changed the drawing in two places:

| affordance | what the code actually does |
|---|---|
| Add a league | **TWO paths.** `app.py:2498` takes a raw league ID (one league, appended). `app.py:2328 sync_leagues(username)` takes an account and REPLACES the list. |
| Delete | `app.py:1438`, real, local, confirmed. **Never touches Sleeper** — a league you are still in reappears unsynced on the next account sync. |
| Leagues you left | already computed by `sync_leagues`' diff; had no surface anywhere |
| Archive / reorder | `league_prefs`, local only; Sleeper has no concept of either |

An earlier draft had only the account path and would have drawn "Add league" as a lie about what
the button does. The delete panel states the purge list and the never-touches-Sleeper line,
because a delete button that reads as *leaving the league* is the most expensive
misunderstanding available on this surface.

**COLLAPSING THE SET-UP HALF, AND WHAT IT COSTS.** Asked whether these would be cleaner as
collapsible commands: yes, for the bottom half. Four always-open cards spent ~700px on the
least-used controls. Folded into four commands the page went **2311px -> 1606px (-30%)**. But
collapsing hides STATE, not just controls — a bare row of verbs would have concealed that
nothing is archived, or that no key is set. Each command therefore carries the one number its
panel reports (`2 archived - 1 left`, `Sleeper - 1 of 3 providers`, `oldest source 62d`).

**THREE DEFECTS, ALL FOUND BY RENDERING IT.** None would have been caught by reading the code.

1. `var(--sans)`/`--mono`/`--display` were **never defined** — `design_system` defines colour
   tokens; the faces are Python constants `round5` substitutes with `.format()`. An
   unresolvable `var()` inside a `font:` SHORTHAND invalidates the whole declaration, so every
   rule setting size and face together was silently dropped. Measured: type scale **12->22px**,
   the 3.4rem tally rendering at **14.24px**. No console error, no warning — a complete,
   plausible page at the wrong size, which is this repo's signature failure mode.
2. A raw Python dict shipped onto the page: `checks_summary` returns a dict BY DESIGN (`#338`)
   and a draft interpolated it directly, printing
   `{'ran': 3, 'clean': ['holes', 'byes', 'depth'], ...}` in a league row.
3. A cascade collision: `.verdict p` (0,1,1) beat `.tally` (0,1,0), crushing the hero figure to
   14.24px. **This survived defect 1's fix** — two independent causes of one symptom, and
   repairing the first made the second look repaired.

**A SIXTH HOLLOW INSTRUMENT, CAUGHT BEFORE IT SHIPPED.** `build_dashboard._assert_type_floor()`
closes over its own module-global `CSS` and takes no argument. Imported and called from a
different builder it checks the DASHBOARD's stylesheet, passes unconditionally, and reports
nothing about the file it appears to guard. Both gates were rewritten here to take their subject
as a parameter. Mutation-checked 4 arms: real call passes; dropping `font_vars()` FIRES;
`.6rem` FIRES; `0.9em` FIRES. The type floor fired on its first real run (`.7rem`, `.74rem`).

Final: scale 12->54px (4.53:1), 18 sizes, min font 12.0px, 0 overflow at 390px, 0 console errors.

**NOT FIXED, AND WHY.** The twelve rows are twelve SEATS of one replayed league, so five read
nearly identically — a fixture artifact, stamped CONSTRUCTED on the page. **This page has never
been seen against leagues that actually differ**, which is the one test that matters for a list
whose entire job is telling leagues apart. Connection state is constructed throughout (no
`data/` on a fresh clone). No test file yet, so `#347` is RECORDED, NOT CLOSED.

### `#348` — THE PROVIDER REGISTRY IS AGNOSTIC; THREE TABLES IN `app.py` ARE NOT

> api keys need to be agnostic, not tied to specific models, companies, etc. if i wanted to
> integrate kimi k2 or grok, that should not fight the language used

`providers.py` already is what the owner is asking for: a frozen `Provider` dataclass with `id`,
`label`, `key_field` and an `is_configured` callable, plus `register()`. The round-7 page
therefore names no provider at all — it reads the registry, so a provider registered tomorrow
appears with no edit. Two facts that reading produced and memory would not have: the registry is
EMPTY at `providers`' own import and populated at `llm_engine`'s (a page that read it too early
renders an empty card and looks correct), and openai's real label is **"ChatGPT"**.

**The page's language was the easy half.** `app.py` holds two tables DERIVED from the registry
(`PROVIDER_KEY_FIELD`, `IS_PROVIDER_CONFIGURED`, lines 1046-1047) and **three hardcoded to the
same three providers**:

| site | what it hardcodes |
|---|---|
| `app.py:770 ENV_VAR_FOR_OVERRIDE` | override field -> env var name |
| `app.py:1050 CREDENTIAL_FIELD_ALIASES` | override field -> accepted `.env` spellings |
| `app.py:3540-3542` | a literal tuple calling `is_claude_configured` / `is_gemini_configured` / `is_openai_configured` **by name** |

The third is the worst: it calls three named functions instead of the `is_configured` callable
the `Provider` already carries, so a registered Grok is invisible to that check even though the
registry knows how to test it. This is `#312`'s "one palette, three homes" in the provider layer.

So registering Kimi K2 or Grok today takes one `providers.register(...)` call **plus edits to
three tables that the registry does not reach** — and missing the first two fails silently: the
paste-a-`.env` flow simply would not recognise the new key. NOT FIXED; this is a repair to
`app.py`, not to a mockup, and it wants its own pass.

### `#349` — THE LANDING PAGE GETS ITS ORNAMENT, AND THE ART PIPELINE THAT PRODUCED IT

Ten commits (`a68c6f5` `52431c5` `d2eaad8` `b05170c` `e055a01` `3e41ae2` `1a01872` `f058c51`
`f517009`), recorded here late. Full detail lives in `ui_explore/round7/ART_BRIEF.md`; this entry
exists so the number resolves and the rulings are findable.

**What the pass established, each measured rather than argued:**

- **The pure-black-void rule.** A generated image must carry `(0,0,0)` corners or it cannot sit on
  the page's ground without a visible seam.
- **The slot was the problem, not the images.** Four band candidates all read as wrong until the
  slot widened; the fifth prompt was not better art, it was art given room. The first league-band
  prompt was **self-contradictory** — "extreme close detail" and "empty left third" cannot both
  hold — and no amount of regeneration would have fixed it.
- **The room-mark set is ABANDONED (`1a01872`), and the reason outlived the marks.** Generated
  marks would not cohere at 19px. The limit turned out to be the FORMAT, not the style
  (`f517009`): raster at that size loses the stroke, so the owner's own suggestion — five simple
  tribal glyphs, drawn as filled SVG — made generation unnecessary. `tribal_glyphs.py`'s
  `assert_legible_sizes()` refuses any stroke, which is the lesson enforced rather than noted.

**CORRECTION, already published at `e055a01` and restated here in full.** I reported the shipped
band's nav contrast as clean at **4.80:1**. That measured ONE tab. All tabs measured **3.34:1** —
below AA. Root cause: `--dim` is 4.82:1 on the flat background, i.e. **zero headroom** for a
clickable label the moment it sits on anything but flat ground. Moved to `--muted` (7.89:1). The
defect in the instrument was sampling one member of a row and reporting the row.

### `#350` — THE IN-LEAGUE DASHBOARD IS WIRED, AND IT COMPOSES NOTHING

Recorded late; shipped at `0869d52`. The page is **assembly only** — every claim on it was composed
by round 5's `front_claims.compose`, which is `#338`'s rule (the render layer computes nothing)
held rather than restated.

**Four defects found by LOOKING at a render, none catchable by a test on the composition:**

1. **A raw Python dict shipped onto a page, twice.** `checks_summary` returns a dict BY DESIGN
   (`#338`: the surface derives no counts) and a draft interpolated it whole. Then `fx["league"]` —
   the league CONFIG, not a name — printed `{'roster_positions': [...], 'starting_slots': 10}` into
   the header. The falsy-guard failed because **a non-empty dict is truthy**. Guard now keys on
   TYPE, never truthiness, and `test_no_python_repr_reaches_the_page` reads the rendered string for
   the fingerprints of an escaped Python value.
2. **`var(--sans)` was never defined.** An unresolvable `var()` inside a `font:` shorthand **drops
   the whole rule silently** — no error, no fallback. The type scale read 12→22px and the tally
   14.24px. Fixed with `font_vars()`; `assert_vars_resolve` now fails the build on it.
3. **A cascade collision, fixed twice.** `.verdict p` beat `.tally`. The first repair
   (`.verdict div p`) was position-dependent and broke the moment the crest was nested inside.
   Re-done as `.verdict .vtext p` — matching, not specificity, so nesting cannot recapture it.
4. **A module importing itself.** Round 7's `build_dashboard.py` resolved `import build_dashboard`
   to itself. Fixed by path-loading — and the mirror image in `build_landing.py` was left in place,
   which cost ten suite errors one commit later. See the certification commit for that.

**The crest rendered as a black square** despite `(0,0,0)` corners and `mix-blend-mode:screen`:
`.roomhead{z-index:2}` creates a stacking context, which **isolates the blend**. Replaced with a
radial mask, which does not depend on compositing order.

### `#351` — TWO SERIALIZATION DEFECTS WEARING ONE NAME, AND A DOCSTRING THAT CONFLATED THEM

**NEW FINDING, and it carries a correction to a pushed artifact.**

`test_priced_travels_with_value.py:116` tells the reader this is *"recorded as `#351`"*. **It was
not.** No entry existed until this one. A committed test file asserting that a finding is recorded
is manufacturing provenance: the next reader goes looking, finds nothing, and cannot tell whether
the record was lost or the claim was false.

**There are TWO mechanisms here, and only one is accidental.** The same docstring attributes both
to `default=str`, which is wrong about the second:

| field | what the file holds | mechanism | deliberate? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `roster[].eligible` | `"{'RB'}"` — a set's repr | `json.dumps(..., default=str)`, `capture_front_fixture.py:253` | **no — side effect** |
| `_provenance.players_db` | a 200-char fragment ending `"s_present': ['"` | `str(prov)[:200]`, `capture_front_fixture.py:201` | **yes — explicit** |

Measured consequence, run rather than reasoned:

    capture_date(<the truncated 200 chars>)  ->  None        # the absence the dashboard renders
    capture_date(<a whole record>)           ->  '2026-09-07'

So the dashboard's absent capture date is **correct behaviour on damaged input** — `ast.literal_eval`
refuses a truncated repr and the page says so rather than regexing a date out of it (`#222`). The
damage is upstream, in the capture.

**What this rules OUT.** The page is not at fault and needs no change. `eligible` is rebuilt by any
consumer that needs it — `test_the_solvers_still_accept_the_row_shape` has to reconstruct the sets
because `bye_collision` does `player["eligible"] & slot["eligible"]` and raises
`TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for &: 'str' and 'set'` on the stored string.

**NOT FIXED, deliberately.** Repairing the serializer changes every fixture's bytes, which means
re-deriving twelve seats and two fixtures and re-certifying every page that reads them. That is its
own pass with its own suite run. The truncation at line 201 is the cheaper half and may be the
better first move: 200 characters was chosen to keep the provenance short, and nobody measured that
it cuts mid-value.

**A CORRECTION I ALMOST PUBLISHED, recorded because the near-miss is the lesson.** While gathering
this evidence I ran `git grep -n 'default=str' -- '*.py' | head` and concluded the capture does not
use `default=str` at all — which would have been a FALSE CORRECTION OF A TRUE CLAIM, worse than the
original error. There are **47** matches; git orders by path; `ui_explore/` sorts after
`measurement.py`; `head` cut the only row that mattered. Third instance this session of a truncated
or sampled result producing a confident answer about something else (the others: nav contrast read
off one tab of eight, `#349`; a halo metric that counted filigree inside the subject as halo).
**Rule: never read a yes/no answer off a truncated result set — count it first.**

### `#352` — A VERIFICATION THAT CANNOT FAIL IS NOT A VERIFICATION, AND A FAILED ONE MUST BE DISCLOSED

**STANDING RULE. Proposed by ChatGPT acting as an architectural reviewer; ADOPTED by the owner on
2026-11-08 because he agrees with it, not because it was proposed.** The provenance is recorded
because a governance rule with no recorded author has the same defect as a finding with no entry.

Two parts, and the second is the one that was earned the hard way:

> **(a)** Verification failures — **including failures of the verification process itself** — must be
> disclosed to whoever is relying on the result.
>
> **(b)** The hardest case is not a check that fails. It is a check that **exits 0 without checking
> anything**, which at the call site is indistinguishable from a pass. So every verification must be
> demonstrated capable of failing before its success is reported.

**THE MEASURED INCIDENT THIS COMES FROM.** In the pre-flight for the second full-suite run I ran
all eight ratchets and published *"all 8 ratchets PASS."* I had run `skip_gates.py` **bare**. With
no arguments it prints its help text and returns 0. It had checked nothing, and the suite then
failed on an unregistered gate the ratchet exists to catch. The claim was already published when
the failure surfaced.

Part (b) is why part (a) is not sufficient alone: a rule that only covers *disclosed failures*
misses this entire class, because nothing failed. Nothing was even examined.

**WHAT THIS BINDS, CONCRETELY.** Every instrument in this repo gets run against a state it should
REJECT before its pass is trusted. Worked examples already in the tree:

- the eight ratchets are run with their real `--check` flags, never bare;
- `test_the_build_gates_can_actually_fail` asserts `SystemExit` from each build gate on sub-floor
  type, an `em` unit, and an undefined `var()`;
- the per-identity accounting script written for this certification was run against the FAILING log
  first and reported `0 of 13`, proving it can fail, before being trusted on a passing one;
- a mutation arm that does not fire is a BUG IN THE ARM, not evidence of a robust test — one in
  this round silently never applied its edit because of quote escaping.

**THE RULE GENERALISES PAST TESTS.** Three findings in this project were withdrawn because the
FIXTURE was wrong while the instrument ran perfectly (`#201`, `#222` twice). Those were not failed
verifications either. They were verifications of something else.
---

### `#353` — `HANDOFF.md` IS THE ONLY HOME SOME ITEMS HAVE, WHICH MAKES IT A REGISTER BY DEFAULT

**STANDING RULE, same provenance as `#352`: proposed in review, adopted by the owner 2026-11-08.**

> - `POST_AUDIT_PLAN.md` is authoritative for numbered findings.
> - `HANDOFF.md` tracks project state, milestones and outstanding work.
> - `HANDOFF.md` MAY reference register IDs. It may NOT become a second findings register.
> - Historical references stay traceable when records are reconciled. Nothing is silently rewritten.

**A CORRECTION TO MY OWN FRAMING OF THIS, MADE BEFORE IT WAS WRITTEN DOWN.** I first described
this as "`HANDOFF.md` became a second findings register." **It did not, and the overstatement
matters because the real defect is narrower and harder to see.** Its rows carry STATE, which is
exactly what the rule above assigns to it:

| `#339` thin_positions cross-interface | **CERTIFIED** 4444 / 1465.001s OK |
| `#343` dashboard | built, 24 tests, 8 ratchets green — **full suite owed** |
| `#345` / `#345b` round 6 | brief + 2 of 3 explorations committed |

Those are states, not findings. The defect is that for `#345` **this is the only record anywhere
that the item exists at all** — so a status table became the sole home for an item's existence,
which makes it a register for that item whether or not it holds the finding. Nothing drifted on
purpose; a gap in one document silently promoted the other.

**THE MEASUREMENT.** Mapping `#340`–`#355` against the register, the commit log and every code
citation:

| item | register entry | commits | cited in code/docs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `#340`–`#344`, `#346`–`#348` | HEADING | — | yes |
| `#345` | **none, ever** | 4 | 2 docstrings + `HANDOFF.md` |
| `#349` | **none** | 10 | `ART_BRIEF.md`, 2 builders |
| `#350` | **none** | 1 | 2 test modules |
| `#351` | **none** | 0 | 1 test module, which claims it IS recorded |

**FOUR STATES OF RECORD INTEGRITY, not three.** The taxonomy this mapping forced:

1. the behaviour exists in the code;
2. something references the item number;
3. the item is formally recorded where the project says authoritative records live;
4. **the item is formally tracked SOMEWHERE ELSE.**

State 4 is more dangerous than a plain gap, because it looks like bookkeeping is happening. `#345`
is in state 4. `#351` is in states 1 and 2 only while *claiming* state 3, which is worse again —
a reader who goes looking cannot tell whether the record was lost or the claim was false.

**THIS IS `#126` TURNED ON THE PROJECT'S OWN RECORD.** The repo already ruled that important
information gets ONE home, and the bookkeeping grew a second one for `#345`. Same family as
`#312`'s three palettes and `#348`'s three provider tables; the novel part is that the duplicated
thing is the record itself.

**NOT DONE BY BULK COPY.** `HANDOFF.md`'s rows are not transplanted. Each gap is established on its
own evidence and recorded as what it actually is — which is why `#345` is written up as a design
exploration rather than promoted to a finding it never was.

### `#353b` — THE RULE HAS NO INSTRUMENT, AND MY FIRST THREE ATTEMPTS TO SIZE THE GAP WERE WRONG

`HANDOFF.md`'s own header already states this rule: *"The register holds the reasoning; this holds
the STATE and the NEXT ACTIONS."* **The rule was written down and the drift happened anyway, because
nothing checked it** — which is `#352` applied to the record. A rule enforced only by prose is the
weak form.

Sizing the gap for a future ratchet took **three instruments, two of which produced confident wrong
answers**, and the sequence is the finding:

| attempt | measured | why it was wrong |
|---|---|---|
| 1. headings only, `head`-truncated grep | — | `\| head` cut the one row that mattered off a 47-row result |
| 2. heading present / absent | **80 unrecorded** | the heading convention is RECENT; early items are recorded in prose and tables, so this measured the convention, not the record. `#187` is cited in 97 files and appears **30 times in the register** — with no heading |
| 3. mentioned anywhere, 1-3 digits | **9 unrecorded** | 6-digit values like `#755024` are HEX COLOURS, not item numbers; the digit bound excludes them |

**The honest figure is 9**, of 221 distinct items cited across tracked `.py` and `.md`:

    #3  #7  #19  #31  #34  #77  #218  #235  #260

Even that is an upper bound — `#3` and `#7` are cited only in `ui_explore/round2/fableA/REVISION.md`
and are probably revision numbers, not items. `#218` is cited only in a skill file.

**SO THE RATCHET IS BUILDABLE AND IS THE NEXT ACTION, NOT THIS ENTRY'S WORK.** The design that
follows from the measurement: count items CITED but never MENTIONED, bound the match to 1-3 digits,
baseline the current population in a tracked JSON and forbid GROWTH — the shape `SKIP_GATES.json`
already uses, because reaching zero would mean inventing entries for items that may not exist.
Shrinkage free, growth fails the build.

**AND THE RULE THIS COST:** *never read a yes/no answer off a truncated result set, and never let a
CONVENTION stand in for the THING.* Both failures here were the same shape as `#222`'s withdrawn
findings — the instrument ran perfectly and measured something else.

### `#354` — SERVER-RENDERED, ONE PROCESS, LOCALHOST FIRST: THE STACK DECISION, RECORDED

**No framework decision existed anywhere in this repo.** `GOLD_WYRM_WEBFRONT.md` argues the
McMaster-Carr case for server-rendered HTML but **explicitly disclaims being a mandate**, and `D7`
concerns the visual reference, not the stack. So every statement about "the rewrite" was resting on
an unrecorded assumption. This entry is that decision, with the measurements it rests on.

**MEASURED, on this container, warm:**

| operation | cost |
|---|---|
| engine warm-up | 0.9 s, **once** |
| `front_claims.compose()` | 0.00 ms median, 0.04 ms worst |
| full dashboard HTML assembly | 0.5 ms median |
| dashboard page size | 221.0 KB raw / 148.4 KB gzip-9 |

**RULING 1 — SERVER-RENDERED HTML, NOT A JSON API.** A JSON API forces a SECOND implementation of
claim composition in JavaScript, which is `#126` (one home) and `#336b` (a renderer inventing a
quantity) by construction. There is no performance argument on the other side: composition is
already free.

**RULING 2 — ONE PROCESS (option A), NOT A WEB SERVER PLUS A WORKER.** The decisive argument is
**not** performance. `app.py` persists state to local files with **no locking and no notion of who
is asking** — the same property that makes one passphrase mean one user. A second process does not
add a worker to that design; it adds a **second writer to unsynchronized files**. One process is an
architectural constraint that currently protects data integrity.

Three things make a single *threaded* process actually safe, since one process alone does not
serialize writes:

1. **atomic writes** — temp file in the same directory, then `os.replace()`, so a reader sees the
   whole old file or the whole new one, never a partial. This is the one that matters most: it
   protects readers **without** requiring them to take a lock.
2. **one lock on the mutate path** — writers serialize; readers never wait.
3. **single-flight** — a sync already running refuses a second rather than queueing it.

**WHAT FORCES A WORKER LATER, already measured:** one 12-team draft is **216–956 s**. Nothing serves
that inside an HTTP request under any framework. When drafting goes behind the URL it becomes a
submitted job with a status endpoint, and *then* the worker is a separate process. Not before —
building it early only doubles the writers before any locking exists.

**RULING 3 — MILESTONE 1 LISTENS ON `127.0.0.1` ONLY.** Owner's ruling, 2026-11-08. The passphrase
gate is **decorative without HTTPS**; authentication is its own milestone. Localhost makes the
patience structural rather than disciplinary: there is no exposed endpoint to get impatient about.
The gate is installed in `app.py` only — the round-7 mockups are fixture-built static HTML and leak
no league data, so a login on them is friction without protection.

**AN ASSET DEFECT THE DECISION EXPOSES.** 83% of the dashboard page is three inlined base64 images:

| | raw | gzip-9 |
|---|---|---|
| 3 data URIs | 183.1 KB | **137.4 KB (75%)** |
| HTML + CSS | 37.9 KB | **9.9 KB (26%)** |

JPEG/PNG/WebP are already compressed, so gzip recovers base64's inflation and stops — 137.4 KB is
essentially the original binary. **Inlining was CORRECT for a file you double-click and wrong the
moment a server exists**, because a data URI cannot be cached. Repair: content-addressed filenames
served `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`.

| | first visit | each navigation after |
|---|---|---|
| today | 148.4 KB | **148.4 KB** |
| content-addressed + cached | 147 KB | **9.9 KB** |

The first visit is a wash. **The entire win is repeat navigation, and it exists only if the cache
headers are right** — so the headers are not a nicety on that task, they ARE the task. Brotli is
NOT measured: neither `brotli` nor `brotlicffi` is installed here, and the expected result is not
a measurement.

**MILESTONE 1 ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA** (adopted from review, with the latency item added): real league
data and no demo fixtures; cold start; warm request; consecutive requests; direct URL navigation and
browser refresh; empty vs populated account; missing or stale source data; no mutation of league
state; **and end-to-end request latency plus real transfer size measured — not composition time,
which is the 0.5 ms figure and was never the request.**
---

## `#355` — THE NINTH RATCHET, AND FIVE OF THE EIGHT COULD NOT FAIL EITHER

`#353` was a rule with no instrument. This is the instrument — and building it found that the
rule's own enforcers had the same defect.

### The ratchet

`register_index.py` counts item numbers CITED in tracked `.py`/`.md` that `POST_AUDIT_PLAN.md`
never mentions, baselines the population in `REGISTER_INDEX.json`, and fails on GROWTH.
`skip_gates`' bargain, not `assertion_floors`': **shrinkage is free, and zero is not the target.**
Driving it to zero would mean inventing entries for items that may not be items — `#3` and `#7`
appear only in a round-2 revision document and are almost certainly revision numbers. Writing an
entry to satisfy a counter is the exact defect `#351` records.

**MEASURED, 5/5 mutation arms against the REAL tree** (a citation appended to a tracked file, the
check run, the file restored — not a mock):

| arm | expected | result |
|---|---|---|
| untouched tree | pass | exit 0 |
| `` `#399` `` cited, never mentioned | **FAIL** | exit 1, names the file |
| `#398` cited WITHOUT backticks | pass (documented blind spot) | exit 0 |
| `` `#755024` `` — a hex colour | pass (not an item) | exit 0 |
| a citation removed | pass (shrinkage is free) | exit 0 |

Arms 3 and 4 are the ones worth having: they prove the documented limits are real rather than
asserted.

### The observer effect, which is why the baseline reads 0

When `#353b` was written it listed the nine then-unmentioned items BY NUMBER while explaining that
they were unmentioned. **Documenting the gap closed the gap as this instrument measures it.** That
is a legitimate closure rather than an accident that hid something — a reader who looks up `#34`
now reaches `#353b`, which states what `#34` is and why it has no entry, and traceability is what
`#353` required. But the number must be read knowing how it got there, and the stated limit is
blunt: **this cannot tell a RECORD from a MENTION-AS-GAP.** No text-matching instrument can. That
is the boundary of what the check is evidence for, not a defect to be fixed inside it.

### A FOURTH SIZING ATTEMPT, MEASURED AND REJECTED

Requiring the register to cite back in BACKTICKS — symmetric with how citations are read — gives
**17** rather than 0, and looked like the stricter, better rule. It is not. **The register uses
both forms**: its headings carry `` `#348` `` and its prose carries a bare `#187`, `#166`, `#174`.
So a backtick requirement measures the register's internal formatting inconsistency, not whether a
record exists — which is attempt 2's error in a new costume, three paragraphs after naming it. The
17 are items the register discusses without backticking them; worth tidying, not worth ratcheting.

### AND THEN THE FINDING THAT WAS NOT THE POINT OF THIS PASS

`#352` says a verification tool must have no zero-exit path that verifies nothing. Measuring the
eight existing ratchets against their own rule:

| ratchet | bare invocation | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `assertion_floors`, `suite_reach`, `prose_names` | bare **is** the check | sound |
| `skip_gates` | printed help, exit 0 | **hollow** |
| `boundary_census`, `api_surface`, `state_vocabulary` | printed a listing, exit 0 | **hollow** |
| `doc_index` | **WROTE `DOC_INDEX.md`**, exit 0 | **self-defeating** |

**Five of eight, not one.** The published claim "all 8 ratchets PASS" was made after running them
bare; it could have been false about any of the five, and was false about `skip_gates`.

`doc_index` is the worst and was the least visible: bare invocation regenerated the very artifact
`--check` compares against, so `doc_index.py && doc_index.py --check` passed **unconditionally**,
whatever had drifted. An unrecognised flag did the same — `doc_index.py --oops` silently rewrote
the index and exited 0. A self-defeating instrument is not a weak check; it is an anti-check, and
it had been in the tree since the ratchet was written.

**All five repaired: bare now runs the check.** Listings moved behind `--list`, `doc_index`'s write
behind `--write` (its generated header and its own stale-message updated to name the flag), and an
unrecognised argument exits 2 rather than writing.

**The guard that keeps it repaired** is `EveryRatchetsBareInvocationRunsItsCheck`, which holds all
nine to the rule. It compares bare OUTPUT against `--check` OUTPUT, not exit codes, and the
distinction is the whole design: **in a green tree a hollow ratchet and a sound one both exit 0,**
which is exactly why the defect survived long enough to be published. Help text and a census
listing do not equal a verdict line. It shells out rather than calling `main` in-process because
the nine do not share a signature — `prose_names.main()` takes no argv — and because the command
line is the surface where the false pass actually happened.

**Mutation-verified:** reverting `skip_gates` bare to `parser.print_help()` fires **2 failures**
and names the culprit. Cost: 39.9s for the module, 2.9% of the suite, spent on the one test that
would have caught the error I published.

### THE FULL SUITE CAUGHT THE NEW RATCHET BREAKING AN OLD CONTRACT

The first full run of this pass returned **1 failure in 4543 tests**, and it was correct:

    FAIL: test_store_io.EveryStoreGoesThroughItTests.test_no_module_writes_a_json_store_outside_store_io
    AssertionError: Lists differ: ['register_index.py:151'] != []

`register_index.write` wrote `REGISTER_INDEX.json` with `write_text(json.dumps(...))`. Every JSON
store in this repo goes through `store_io.write`, which replaces the file ATOMICALLY and **returns
a bool because it can decline** -- it refuses to overwrite a store it reads as damaged (`#52`
phase 7.5). `skip_gates` and `assertion_floors` both already route their baselines that way; the
new one did not, because I wrote it from the shape of the problem rather than from the shape of
its neighbours.

Routed through `store_io.write`, and the returned bool is NOT ignored: a declined write now raises
rather than returning a baseline that never reached disk. Ignoring it is the measured defect that
bool exists for -- `upload_batches.record` once returned a batch id for a batch that was never
written, while the interface reported success.

Worth stating plainly because it is the whole argument for the full-suite rule: **every targeted
check passed before this run.** Nine ratchets green with real flags, 12 new tests green, 5/5
mutation arms green against the real tree. The defect was in a contract the new file had no reason
to know about, held by a test module it never touches. That is `#144`'s failure mode exactly, and
the only thing standing between it and a push was the step that takes 23 minutes.

### What is NOT fixed

The 17 backtick-inconsistent citations are left alone, deliberately — tidying them is a formatting
pass and this instrument has no business ratcheting a convention. `test_skip_gates.py` and
`test_boundary_census.py` still never call their own `main()`, which is why the hollow path
survived in them; the new guard covers the bare-invocation property for all nine, but their mains
remain otherwise untested by their own modules.

## `#356` / `#357` — MILESTONE 1: THE SEAM IS WIRED, AND THE ABSENCE CONTRACT CAN MASK A WIRING ERROR

Owner's rulings (`#354`): server-rendered, one process, **127.0.0.1 only**, gate on `app.py` only.
Milestone 1 proves the seam; it does not deliver the dashboard.

### `#356` — THE DEFECT THE VOCABULARY EXISTS FOR

`#187` makes an absence render as an em dash CARRYING ITS REASON. That protects a reader from an
invented number and gives them **nothing at all** against a field that should have arrived and did
not. Read the wrong Sleeper key and `league.name` is `None`, and the page prints

    — (this capture carries a league CONFIG but no league name)

**which is indistinguishable from the contract working perfectly.** The owner loads their league,
sees a tidy labelled absence, and cannot tell it from a bug. This matters here more than anywhere
because I CANNOT VERIFY THIS AGAINST THEIR LEAGUE: `data/sleeper_snapshots/` holds nothing but a
`.gitkeep`, and the committed league captures carry settings with no rosters. The page has to be
the instrument.

So `live_source.py` labels every field with WHY it is entitled to be missing:

| state | meaning | renders as |
|---|---|---|
| `measured` | the source supplied it | the value |
| `structurally_absent` | this source genuinely cannot supply it | em dash + reason (`#187`) |
| `read_failed` | the source OWES it and it did not arrive | **loud banner, never an em dash** |
| `not_computed` | supplied, but a derived claim was deliberately not built | the reason |

`None` looks identical in all four, so the distinction cannot come from the data. It comes from
`EXPECTS` — per SOURCE KIND, the fields that source owes. A snapshot owes a league name because
every Sleeper league has one; a fixture does not, because a replayed draft never had one. It is
data rather than conditionals so a reader can check it against Sleeper's API in one sitting.

**FIVE FIELDS FLIP on a real league**, which is why they are exactly the ones a wiring error hides
in: `current_week`, `league_name`, `record`, `starters`, `team`. The round-7 dashboard references
`starters` **zero times** and `league_name` zero times — there was never anything to draw.

### A DEFECT THIS BRIDGE SHIPPED IN ITS FIRST DRAFT, CAUGHT BY RUNNING IT

`checks_run`'s docstring states the grammar and names the mistake in advance:

> `[]` is a measured empty result — holes were counted, there were none — while a missing key or
> `None` never ran. **A caller that hands `[]` for something it did not measure has broken the
> absence contract at the producer, and that is its defect to fix, not this function's to guess
> around.**

The first draft wrote `"thin_positions": []`. `checks_run` duly reported the depth check **CLEAN
on a check that had never run** — so a league with no structural holes would have rendered
"nothing open" with two of three checks never performed. Omitted rather than emptied, and pinned
end to end: `ran=1`, `absent=['byes','depth']`, `all_clean=False`.

### `bye_profile` REFUSES AN UNPRICED ROSTER, AND THE REFUSAL IS IN THE CODE

`bye_collision` negates `value` to build a maximisation, so an unpriced roster — every row at the
neutral `0.0` that `#346` requires — returns `value_lost: 0.0` for **every week**. A
measured-looking zero meaning "nothing was priced": `#346`'s defect through a different door. The
guard refuses unless every row is priced, so a caller cannot reach the wrong answer by forgetting.
Pricing is not wired in this pass, so `structural_holes` is the one claim a snapshot supplies —
`slot_coverage` takes no `value` by design, because legality in a slot has nothing to do with price.

### `#357` — WHAT THE SERVER MEASURED

Starlette + uvicorn (both already installed; no FastAPI, no pydantic). Four routes: `/`,
`/status`, `/league/{id}`, `/fixture/{name}`. **It writes nothing** — pinned by a source scan with
its own non-vacuity control, because that is the single property making it safe beside `app.py`'s
unsynchronised single writer.

| | measured |
|---|---|
| warm-up (6,594 players + merger) | **once**, ~450ms on first request |
| `compose()` | 0.00ms median, 0.04ms worst |
| page assembly | 0.5ms |
| **full HTTP request, end to end** | **1.7–3.2ms, median ~2.0ms** |
| transfer | **226,303 bytes** |

**LOOPBACK-ONLY VERIFIED EMPIRICALLY, not from the bind argument:** `127.0.0.1:8765` served 200
while the container's own `192.0.2.2:8765` returned HTTP 000, refused.

The end-to-end figure is the one that was missing. Composition was never the request: HTTP and the
socket add ~1.5ms over it, and on any real network the 226KB dominates both.

### GZIP WAS ADDED AND THE MEASUREMENT ARGUES AGAINST IT

Starlette compresses nothing by default. Turning it on:

    plain   226,303 bytes    3.6 ms
    gzip    151,936 bytes   11.5-12.0 ms

74KB bought for ~8ms of CPU — and milestone 1 is **loopback only**, where those 74KB cost nothing
to send. **On this binding gzip is a net latency loss**, and quoting the byte count without the
clock would be hiding half the result. It stays because it is right the moment there is a network
and 12ms is imperceptible either way, but the order was wrong: 83% of this page is three inlined
base64 images, and JPEG/PNG/WebP are already compressed, so gzip is paying full price to recover
base64's inflation and nothing more. **Content-address those three first** — the HTML drops to
~38KB, where gzip reaches ~10KB almost free. I optimised the part that cannot be compressed.

### WHAT IS NOT BUILT

- **Pricing**, so `bye_profile` and `thin_positions` are `not_computed` on a snapshot. They need
  `depth_chart.positional_depth` over a merger-backed priced pool, with `set_league_format` called
  first or the league's own scoring never reaches a price (`#192`/`#204`).
- **The asset repair.** Content-addressed filenames, `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000,
  immutable`. 148.4KB per navigation becomes 9.9KB after the first — but the win is caching, not
  compression, and it exists only if the headers are right. The builders inline by design so the
  committed pages stay double-clickable, so this needs a mode switch, not a replacement.
- **The landing page over HTTP.** `build_landing.build(fx, seats)` wants the twelve-seat shape; a
  live leagues list is its own bridge.
- **Brotli.** Neither `brotli` nor `brotlicffi` is installed. Unmeasured, and an expected result
  is not a measurement.
- **`app.py` is untouched.** It remains the only writer, and the gate is not installed yet.
---

## `#358` / `#359` — THE ASSET REPAIR, PRICING, AND TWO VACUOUS TESTS I SHIPPED AND REPAIRED

### `#358` — inlined images become content-addressed URLs AT RENDER TIME

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| dashboard HTML | 221.0 KB | **38.0 KB** |
| gzipped | 148.4 KB | **9.9 KB** |
| first visit | 148.4 KB | 147.2 KB |
| **every navigation after** | **148.4 KB** | **9.9 KB** |

**15x on repeat navigation**, confirmed over HTTP: the real server went from 151,936 bytes to
**10,165**. Three assets served with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`.

`immutable` is honest ONLY because the name is the content hash — change the image and the URL
changes, so a stale entry is unreachable rather than wrong. The two halves are one decision.

**IT RUNS AT RENDER TIME, NOT IN THE BUILDERS**, and that was the second design. A mode switch
inside `asset_data_uri` would risk `PagesRebuildIdentically` (which exists because `#332` shipped
27 of 29 stale pages) for a benefit the committed files never receive — they are STANDALONE
artifacts and should inline. It would also put global state inside a builder called from a
threaded server, and give `#126`'s one home for "asset or nothing" a second behaviour.
Externalising afterwards makes the whole repair a pure function of the rendered string.

**A VACUOUS TEST I SHIPPED, caught by its own mutation arm.**
`test_undecodable_base64_is_not_rewritten` used `!!!!notbase64!!!!` — characters OUTSIDE base64's
alphabet, so `DATA_URI` never matched, `swap` was never called, and the decode guard it claims to
exercise was **unreachable**. It passed, and a mutation breaking that guard survived it. `AAAAA`
is five characters of legal alphabet that matches and then fails on length. The repaired test
asserts the payload matches the pattern FIRST, so it can never go vacuous the same way again.

### `#359` — pricing, assembled in PRODUCTION'S shape

`set_league_format` **before anything is priced**, with the hint DERIVED from the league's own
settings. `rec` and `bonus_rec_te` do not propagate through `scoring_settings` into valuation —
they propagate by FILE SELECTION, and a battery that skipped this returned standard / half_ppr /
ppr byte-identical with nine of thirteen findings artifacts. A live league supplies its own
`scoring_settings`, which is `#341`'s currency ruling finally reaching a price.

**MEASURED END TO END on a synthetic snapshot of real players:** 15/15 priced, bye_profile
present, **all three checks ran** (`absent=[]`), one claim fired.

And the detail that proves `#346` defect 2 on live data: the raw profile's worst week is **5 with
a loss of 33.0**, while the CLAIM reports **week 14, loss 32.0** — because week 5 is behind
`current_week=10`, so `byes_ahead` re-picks from the weeks still ahead. Futurity works.

**A `#126` DEFECT IN MY OWN BRIDGE, found by measurement.** `roster_rows` spelled the player name
inline as `full_name or last_name or id`. `pu.player_name` is the one home and falls back to
**first+last BEFORE the id**, so every player without a `full_name` — a team defense, anyone
stored as first/last — got the raw Sleeper id as its name, a string `merge_player` can never
match. Measured on a roster chosen so every member IS in the rankings: **11 of 15 priced where
`player_name` prices 15.** Four rows silently unpriced, each then a measured-looking 0.0 the bye
guard has to refuse. Routed to its one home.

**THE SECOND VACUOUS TEST, and it is the same shape.** The test pinning that fix asserted on a
player WITH a `full_name` — where both spellings agree — so a mutation reintroducing the inline
version SURVIVED it. The fixture now carries a player with no `full_name`, which is the only row
where the two derivations part company. Both vacuous tests were caught by mutation arms that
should have fired and did not; neither would have been caught by running the suite.

**THE MERGER IS MUTATED, SO PRICING TAKES A LOCK.** `set_league_format` selects a different
rankings export — it is a WRITE to shared state, from a threaded server. `#354` chose one process
to protect unsynchronised files, and this is the reminder that **one process does not mean
serialised writes once threads are involved**. Every priced read takes `Engine._price_lock`;
readers of already-rendered pages never touch it.

### WHAT IS STILL NOT BUILT

The live landing page (`build_landing` wants the twelve-seat shape). Brotli — still not installed,
still unmeasured. The gate. `app.py` is untouched and remains the only writer. And nothing here
has been run against a real Sleeper snapshot, because none exists in this container: the owner
has a tunnel at `draft.goldwyrm.com` pointing at `127.0.0.1:8765` on their laptop, which is where
that verification will happen. **A tunnel route publishes a hostname; it is not an Access policy**
— without one under Zero Trust, the hostname is reachable by anyone who knows it.
---

## `#360` — THE TENTH RATCHET CAUGHT A LIVE BREACH: A BORROWED PRICE ON THE ROSTER PATH

**The first live breach `invariant_registry.py` has ever caught.** Every member of this
population before it was judged and found conforming; this one was not.

### What happened

Suite 8 returned **4 failures in 4587 tests**, all in `test_invariant_registry` — a ratchet whose
existence I did not know about. Its census for *"a contested identity's borrowed price is refused
on every path"* moved **10 -> 11**, and the new member was `live_source.py:388` — my `price_rows`.

The population note had described the defect in advance, in the past tense:

> the roster path decided differently from the pool and handed a drafted player the very number
> the board refused him — and it did that through a **DIRECT `merge_player` call**, which a census
> over the conforming name alone could not see.

`price_rows` was a direct `merge_player` call on the roster path. Same defect, same shape, new
file.

### MEASURED, on the committed rankings

    merge_player('Bijan Robinson', RB, ATL) -> trade_value = 99.0
    merge_player('Brian Robinson', RB, ATL) -> trade_value = 99.0

    through price_rows, BEFORE:   Bijan 99.0 priced=True
                                  Brian 99.0 priced=True

Two real men, one `B Robinson RB ATL` vendor row, and no name/position/team test can split them.
`_drop_contested_identities` refuses that number to both. My path handed it to both — and
`bye_collision` would then have counted a value belonging to exactly one of them **twice**.

    AFTER:   Bijan 0.0 priced=False
             Brian 0.0 priced=False
             Patrick Mahomes 28.0 priced=True

**The price is declined, the player is not** (`#196`). The row keeps its identity, its
eligibility and its bye; it is simply unpriced, which the solvers already handle and the page
already renders honestly.

### THE POPULATION THE CONTEST IS COUNTED OVER

**Every player identified in the league, not the one roster being rendered.** Counting over the
rendered roster would reproduce the original defect exactly — the note says *"the contest itself
evaporated as soon as either player was drafted, because it was counted over available rows"* —
and the common case is that the other claimant sits on somebody else's roster.

**RESIDUE, STATED RATHER THAN ACCEPTED SILENTLY:** this is still narrower than the pool's, which
counts over the identified universe. A contest with a player on NO roster in this league is
invisible to it. Smaller than the defect it replaces, and not zero.

### THE REGISTRY CAUGHT MY REPAIR TOO

The fix added `contested_keys`, a second resolution site — so the census moved **11 -> 12** and
made me judge that one as well. That is the mechanism working rather than a nuisance: a guard is
also a place that resolves a player, and it would itself be a place to decide if it ever read a
number rather than a key. It reads only `match_canonical_key`.

The registry has no `--write`, by design: *"Re-verify the claim over the NEW population, THEN
update `census`. Updating the number first is how a registry becomes a rubber stamp."* Both moves
were verified before the number changed, and the first verification FAILED, which is the only
reason this entry exists.

### WHY NO EARLIER STEP COULD HAVE FOUND THIS

Nine ratchets green with real flags. 44 new tests green. 4/4 mutation arms green. The defect lived
in an invariant held by a module my new code never imports, over a population my new code had
silently joined. **The full suite is the only thing that reaches it** — and the suite reached it
only because somebody had previously written down which population each invariant was proven over.
